bio.en: Noah Weiss is Chief Product Officer at Slack, where he has spent the last seven years, after previously serving as Head of Product at Foursquare and as a product manager at Google and Fog Creek.
bio.zh: Noah Weiss 是 Slack 的首席产品官（CPO），已在那里工作七年，此前曾任 Foursquare 的产品负责人，以及 Google 与 Fog Creek 的产品经理。

summary.en: Noah shares the ten traits of great product managers and how to collaborate effectively with strong, product-minded founders. He explains the 'Complaint Storm' process Slack uses to surface and act on user frustration, and reflects on turning around Slack's self-serve business after it plateaued in 2019. The conversation also covers how he thinks about AI in product after 15 years across Google, Foursquare, and Slack, plus lessons on competing with Microsoft Teams and Discord.
summary.zh: Noah 分享了优秀产品经理的十大特质，以及如何与强势且具备产品思维的创始人高效协作。他介绍了 Slack 用来收集并响应用户情绪的“吐槽风暴（Complaint Storm）”流程，并反思了 2019 年自助业务陷入瓶颈后如何实现逆转。对话还涵盖他基于在 Google、Foursquare 和 Slack 共 15 年经验对产品中 AI 的思考，以及应对 Microsoft Teams 和 Discord 竞争的经验。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: We have this mental metaphor that we talk a lot about, getting to the next hill. The actual wording is "Take bigger boulder bets." I think teams can often get lost crawling up that hill, not realizing that there's a huge, incredibly beautiful range behind it where we've over time freighted new teams from scratch that incubated in a new area before the areas mature.
turns.zh: 我们有一个心智隐喻，经常聊到，就是『爬到下一座山头』。确切的说法是『下更大胆的赌注』（Take bigger boulder bets）。我觉得团队常常会在爬那座山时迷失，没意识到它背后还有一片巨大、美得惊人的山脉——我们在那些领域成熟之前，随着时间推移，从零组建了新的团队，让它们在新区里孵化。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: We did that with a lot of these native audiovisual products like huddles and clips really in the pandemic because our customers were demanding it from us. I think in the AI space, we're trying to hear from customers, what do you wish Slack could do if it had these new superpowers? Let's incubate a couple teams or prototype, give them space to run and pilot and then get something to launch that's amazing. Blows people away. That's the formula that we've seen.
turns.zh: 我们在大流行期间，就是这么做的——针对一大批原生的影音产品，比如 huddles 和 clips，因为客户在向我们强烈要求。我觉得在 AI 领域，我们在试着听客户的声音：如果 Slack 有了这些新超能力，你希望它能做什么？我们孵化几个团队、或者做个原型，给他们空间去跑、去试点，然后做出一个能发布的、惊人东西。把人惊艳到。这就是我们见过的公式。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me ask you a question. What advice do you have for someone about to enter the beginning of baby life from someone that is exiting that and going back to work?
turns.zh: 让我问你一个问题。从一个正要走出那段、回到工作的人的角度，你对一个即将进入育儿初期的人，有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: First off, I mean obviously congratulations, you're about to go on. A rollercoaster of emotion, sleep and everything else. I literally went back to work two days ago. I think my, maybe, advice about being a new parent is better than my advice about being at PM right now. Here are the three ... My wife and I wind up coming up with three maxims that we want to be using throughout the first two months to keep ourselves grounded.
turns.zh: 首先，当然要恭喜你，你马上就要开始了。一段情绪、睡眠、以及一切的其他东西的大起大落。我 literally 两天前才回去工作。我觉得，我关于『当个新手上父母』的建议，可能比我此刻关于当 PM 的建议更好。有这么三条……我和我太太最后总结出了三条格言，想在前两个月里一直用，好让我们自己稳住。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: First one, I would say a little bit better every day. No matter how many books you read and how much money ouster you consume, there's nothing like actually doing it. It's a physical thing being a new parent. Getting a little bit better every day, giving yourself permission to be like that didn't go great and that's okay. That's number one.
turns.zh: 第一条，我会说，每天好一点点。无论你读了多少本书、消化了多少课程，都没法和真正去做相比。当个新手上父母，是件身体力行的事。每天好一点点，允许自己承认『那次搞得不太好』，而那没关系。这是第一条。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Number two, don't over extrapolate from the early days. The fourth trimester is a real thing. These babies come out. They're not fully baked. They can't even support their own heads. If you try to extrapolate everything, the next 18 years are going to be the first 18 days, it's going to be sobering. Keep that perspective. They develop so much every week, part of the fun.
turns.zh: 第二条，别从最初那几天过度外推。『第四孕期』是真实存在的。这些宝宝生出来，还没完全长好，连自己的头都撑不住。如果你试图把一切外推，那接下来的 18 年就会是头 18 天，那会让人清醒得难受。保持那个视角。他们每星期都进展那么多，那本身就是乐趣的一部分。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Then the third thing, which I got advice from this from a good friend is like you got to fully get into it as a parent. There's nothing that replaces. Actually, you got to change the diapers. You got to do the feeds. When they're up, even though they can't talk, you got to talk to them. You got to listen to what they're saying and just be fully present near the moment.
turns.zh: 然后第三条，是我从一位好朋友那儿得来的建议：作为父母，你得完全投入进去。没有什么能替代这个。说真的，你得换尿布。你得喂奶。他们醒着的时候，哪怕他们还不会说话，你也得对他们说话。你得听他们『说』的，并且在那一刻完全在场。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I realized for myself, and then basically at full digital detox. You saw how long it took for me to reply to your emails. I was like, "Throw the devices away. Just fully with our daughter, [inaudible 00:06:34], and our family." I feel like it was so much more rewarding. I felt really connected with her now after these couple months. It's a crazy time. You're going to really love it. It's going to drive you mad at that times as well. That's all of it.
turns.zh: 我对自己有这个觉悟之后，基本上就进入了彻底的数字断舍离。你也看到了，我回你邮件花了多久。我当时就想：『把那些设备扔掉。就完全和我们女儿、[inaudible 00:06:34]、和我们家人在一起。』我觉得那要有回报得多。这几个月下来，我现在觉得和她真的有连接。那是一段疯狂的时光。你会真的爱死它。它有些时候也会把你逼疯。就这些了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. We're going to be pivoting this podcast into a parenting podcast. This is awesome advice. I wrote everything you just said on this little post-it as you're talking. I'm going to put that up in our nursery and see how it all goes. One thing that's tough about my career path in this weird life is I don't get a nice pat leave, paid pat leave from a big company.
turns.zh: 好吧。我们要把这档播客转型成育儿播客了。这建议太棒了。你讲的时候，我把你刚说的每句话都写在这张小便利贴上了。我要把它贴到我们育儿室里，看看一切会怎样。我这段怪人生里，职业路径上有件难事：我没法从大公司拿到优厚的陪产假、带薪陪产假。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've actually been working on stacking guest post and podcast ahead of my leave so that I can actually, as exactly as you said, just get fully into it.
turns.zh: 其实我一直在提前囤积客座文章和播客，赶在我休假之前，这样我就能——就像你刚说的——真的完全投入进去。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Smart.
turns.zh: 聪明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I have awesome guest posts coming. All these podcasts are backlogged, so I'm hoping it all works out.
turns.zh: 对。我有超棒的客座文章要发。所有这些播客都排着队呢，所以我盼着一切都能成。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: That's a smart way to do it. Yeah.
turns.zh: 那是聪明的做法。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On a totally different topic, you're ahead of product at Foursquare. I don't know if you know this. I actually built a startup on Foursquare's API. It's a company called Localmind. For folks that don't know about it, the way it worked is basically let you talk to someone, checked in on Foursquare anywhere in the world if you're thinking about going there.
turns.zh: 聊个完全不一样的话题，你曾在 Foursquare 管产品。我不知道你知不知道。我其实在 Foursquare 的 API 上建过一个创业公司。叫 Localmind。给不知道的人说一下，它的运作方式基本是：如果你正考虑去某个地方，它能让你和在世界上任何地方的、在 Foursquare 签到了那儿的人聊上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You could be like, "Hey, is this bar fun right now? What's happening there?" Before you actually show up. We ended up selling the company to Airbnb. Ended up not being a big problem for enough people and that's how I ended up at Airbnb. But it was quite magical and API was amazing. I guess I just want to say thank you for building an awesome product and awesome API.
turns.zh: 你可能会像：『嘿，这酒吧现在好玩吗？那儿在搞什么？』在你真正出现之前。我们最后把公司卖给了 Airbnb。最后它没成为足够多人的大问题，而那就是我怎么到了 Airbnb 的。但它相当有魔力，而且 API 很惊艳。我想我只是想说，谢谢你打造了一款超棒的产品和超棒的 API。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Thank you for being a developer on top of the ecosystem. I mean it's interesting with Foursquare. I will talk about this I'm sure later. I feel like I have more lessons learned and more scar tissue from the crazy up and down of ... I don't know what. It was 2010 to 2015 roughly. I think there's something actually where you learn more from the things that don't fully work out or don't quite achieve what you wanted to achieve.
turns.zh: 谢谢你作为生态之上的开发者。我是说，Foursquare 这事儿挺有意思。我后面肯定会聊到。我觉得我从那忽上忽下的疯狂里，学到了更多教训、也有了更多伤疤——我不知道怎么形容。大概是 2010 到 2015 年。我觉得有件事是真的：你从那些没完全成、或者没完全达成你目标的事里，学到的反而更多。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: You actually have a feedback loop where you get a lot of negative signal about like, "Okay. That didn't work. That didn't work. What can I actually learn, take away from that?" It's still great. I still love using Foursquare. I think we got caught in the death star of Instagram's ascent back in 2012, 2013. But I hope a product like that exists forever in the future and I'm glad you got to build the company, landed Airbnb through it. It's a great story.
turns.zh: 你其实有个反馈回路，会收到很多负面信号，像：『好，那没成。那没成。我到底能学到什么、带走什么？』那依然很棒。我依然爱用 Foursquare。我觉得我们是栽进了 Instagram 在 2012、2013 年崛起的那个死星里。但我希望那样的产品在未来永远存在，而且我很高兴你得以建立那家公司、并借此落脚 Airbnb。这是个很棒的故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Looking back at Foursquare, do you think there was a path to building a massive consumer app type business or is that just never going to work out? I know they went in direction of B2B data business. I guess was there a path or was it just like, "No. That was never going to work out?"
turns.zh: 回头看 Foursquare，你觉得有没有一条路能建成一个庞大的消费级应用类生意，还是说那根本就走不通？我知道他们后来走向了 B2B 数据生意的方向。我猜，是有那么条路，还是说它就只是像：『不。那从来就走不通？』

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: It's tricky. I mean I'm not going to do 30-minute post, because I probably bore everyone. But it's not about this. We've all thought about this a lot on the early team there. I think the biggest probably lesson learned, frankly, is that we were really close with the Instagram folks early on. They were big developers on our platform. They used the Foursquare API before they were bought by Facebook.
turns.zh: 这挺棘手的。我是说，我不会来个 30 分钟的长篇，因为那大概会让人听烦。但这不在点上。我们早期团队里的所有人都想过很多。我觉得，坦白讲，最大的教训大概是：我们早期和 Instagram 那帮人走得很近。他们是我们平台上很大的开发者。他们在被 Facebook 收购之前，就用着 Foursquare 的 API。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think in hindsight we were a little bit mistaken to believe that the idea that the atomic unit would be a person talking about a place that they're at and you have to have a physical place to tie it to versus a person sharing a moment or an experience that they're having in the world. Sometimes that might have a place connected to it.
turns.zh: 我觉得事后看来，我们有点误信了那个想法：原子单位会是一个人在谈论他所在的、而且你必须有个实体场所才能绑定的地点，相对地，是一个人分享他在世界上正拥有的某个时刻或体验。有时那可能会连着一个地点。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think that one change in framer on what you would say a customer actually wanted to do, that probably was the thing that took this away on the social side. I think on the more local discovery side, it's actually what people wind up be using the product much more for over time getting personalized recommendations and getting tips when you go to a place and all the push notifications.
turns.zh: 我觉得，在『一个客户真正想做的』上，那个框架上的转变，大概就是让它在社交侧出局的东西。我觉得在更偏本地发现的那一侧，人们随着时间推移，其实越来越多地用这个产品，是为了获得个性化的推荐、以及去一个地方时拿到贴士、还有各种推送通知。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Again, it was hard to stay ahead, I think specifically of Google, because they had billion plus Google Maps users distributed on Android and iOS. Even though they might only take a couple years, eventually they would wind up replicating a lot of the functionality and then I think it was hard to regain that momentum. Much of this stuff is luck and timing and just coincidences of history.
turns.zh: 再说一次，要保住领先很难，我觉得 specifically 对 Google 而言，因为他们有超过十亿的 Google 地图用户，分布在 Android 和 iOS 上。哪怕他们可能只花几年，最终也会把大量功能复制出来，然后我觉得就很难重拾那个势头了。这类事很多是运气、时机、以及纯粹的历史巧合。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think there was a path. I think in the end we lost their social sales and then Google was able to catch up on the utility side. Now the company's built a really valuable B2B API company which offers a story. I mean Slack is in some ways a pivot, obviously, from a consumer company to a B2B company. But that that's my mini postmortem, what could have been with Foursquare.
turns.zh: 我觉得是有一条路的。我觉得最后我们丢了他们的社交势头，然后 Google 在实用那一侧赶了上来。如今这家公司已经建成了一家很有价值的 B2B API 公司，这本身就是个故事。我是说，Slack 某种程度上显然也是一次转型——从消费级公司转到 B2B 公司。但那是我小小的复盘，关于 Foursquare 本可能成为什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how many consumer companies pivot to B2B because it turns out that's where the money ends up being.
turns.zh: 有意思，这么多消费级公司都转向 B2B，因为到头来钱是在那儿。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. I think the feedback to you get from our people willing to pay for the product that you're building is so much faster than can I build a large-scale consumer business and when they hope to have enough reach to then slap ads onto it. That's a much more of a try to hit a home run and hope it works out. But you don't really know if you're doing it along the way. Yeah. I think B2B is a easier to have a more incremental, successfully business than pure consumer.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得，从那些愿意为你正在打造的产品付钱的人那儿得到的反馈，比『我能建一个大规模的消费级生意、并盼着有足够触达、然后往上面贴广告』要快得多。后者更像是一种试图本垒打、并盼着它能成。但一路上你其实并不知道自己在不在正轨上。对。我觉得 B2B 比纯消费级更容易做出一个更渐进、更成功的生意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Speaking of Foursquare, Dennis Crowley was the CEO and founder, a very strong product-minded founder. I know you've worked with a number of very strong product-minded founders including Stewart Butterfield, Dennis, obviously we just talked about, maybe others. I'm curious what you've learned as a product leader working with very opinionated founders.
turns.zh: 好。说到 Foursquare，Dennis Crowley 是 CEO 兼创始人，一位非常强势、有产品思维的创始人。我知道你和好几位非常强势、有产品思维的创始人合作过，包括 Stewart Butterfield、刚刚聊过的 Dennis，也许还有别人。我好奇，作为一个产品负责人，和这些态度强硬、主意已定的创始人合作，你学到了什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think this is interesting not just as a product leader working with very product-minded CEOs, but also as a first PM at a startup you're often put in this tough spot of just the founders just telling you what to do and you have to go build it versus having a lot of say in agency. I'm curious what you've learned about working and being successful in that position, which is often really hard.
turns.zh: 我觉得这有意思，不只对作为产品负责人、和非常有产品思维的 CEO 合作而言，也对一个创业公司的首位 PM 而言——你常被放在那个尴尬位置上：创始人就告诉你该做什么，你得去造，而不是在决策上有很多发言权。我好奇，关于在那个位置上工作并成功，你学到了什么，那通常真的很难。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I would say to folks in general, if you're joining company and the CEO does the role that is your functional area of expertise, it's probably the area where you'll learn the most because they're hopefully world class at it. But also, one will you'll be the most frustrated at times because you're going to feel like you have less agency. You should just know that going into it.
turns.zh: 我会概括地告诉人们：如果你加入一家公司，而 CEO 正是做你那个专业职能领域的，那大概就是你学得最多的领域，因为他们希望在那上是世界级的。但同时，那也会是你有时最沮丧的领域，因为你会觉得自己的自主权变少了。你在进入之前就该知道这一点。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: If you go to company to run by a former marketer and you're in marketing, they'll probably want to have a lot of say and influence over that. I think just going into knowing that is good. Looking back, I would say probably two main things stand out of what's really worked with both Dennis and Stewart, not just for me but I think for the teams that work with him as well.
turns.zh: 如果你去一家由前市场人运营的公司、而你做市场，他们大概会想在那一摊上有很多发言权和影响力。我觉得，进去之前就知道这点，是好事。回头看，我会说，和 Dennis 与 Stewart 真正奏效的，大概有两点最突出——不只对我，我想对那些和他们共事的团队也是。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: The first is, I think as much as possible, I think maybe we'll talk about this a little bit later as well, is getting to the point where you have alignment on the principles for what it means to build a great product of that company. Not just about if the intuition and tasting gut, but how do you distill that to principles that become the language of the company so that everybody else can start thinking through a similar frame or similar lens when you're designing a product.
turns.zh: 第一点是，我觉得尽可能是：达到那样一个状态——你们对『打造这家公司的好产品意味着什么』的原则，达成对齐。不只是凭直觉和味觉般的 gut（直觉），而是你如何把那个提炼成原则，成为公司的语言，好让其他人在设计产品时，能透过类似的框架或类似的透镜去思考。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Because otherwise it can feel a little bit Goldilocks every time a team builds something, they take it to the CEO. CEO is like, "No, not quite right. Again, no, not exactly that." Then you don't have the language to actually have a more constructive review. Then doing that at the little strategy as well. I think the product founder CEO is always going to be the holder of the vision for the company. I'm sure at Airbnb. I imagine Brian was very much like that as well.
turns.zh: 因为否则的话，每次一个团队做出点什么、拿去给 CEO，都会有种『金发姑娘』（总是不满意）的感觉。CEO 会像：『不，不太对。又不对，不是那个。』然后你们就没有那种语言，去进行更有建设性的评审。然后在小战略层面也这么做。我觉得，产品型的创始人 CEO，永远会是公司愿景的持有者。我敢说在 Airbnb 也是这样。我想象 Brian 也非常像那样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think it's actually great to say, "Okay. The overall vision for the company, is it the responsibility of any one team to have everyone buy into that vision, but then to have space for teams to be able to actually do creative work, do explorations because you know that it's aligned with that high level vision."
turns.zh: 我觉得其实很好地说：『好。公司的整体愿景，是任何一个团队的责任，要让所有人都买账那个愿景；但接下来，要留给团队空间，让他们能真正做创造性的工作、做探索，因为你知道那与那个高层级的愿景是对齐的。』

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: If you can get that alignment and you can get those principles as the common language of what creative software looks like, I think you can have a really good working relationship. Then the other bit I would just say is I think when to involve the founder CEO in a project is really important. The short version I think that works the best is almost like a U-curve where the X-axis is time and the Y-axis is level of involvement.
turns.zh: 如果你能拿到那个对齐、并且把那些原则变成『有创造力的软件长什么样』的共同语言，我觉得你就能拥有一段很好的工作关系。然后另一点我想说的是：我觉得，何时让创始人 CEO 介入一个项目，真的很重要。我觉得最好使的简短版本，差不多像一条 U 形曲线——横轴是时间，纵轴是介入程度。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think you want to get the founder CEO really involved early on, especially if it's a big new project, to make sure that there's strategic buy-in that you agree on the principle strategy and approaching you agree on the goals and the anti-goals, getting that to then the team can run and explore. Then I think at the very end you want them to really be bought in that did you build something that's up to the quality ... the company?
turns.zh: 我觉得你想让创始人 CEO 在早期就深度介入，尤其如果是个重大的新项目，好确保有战略上的认同——你们在原则、战略、切入方式上达成一致，在目标和反目标上也达成一致——拿到那个之后，团队才能去跑、去探索。然后我觉得，在非常末端，你想让他们真正买账：你造出的东西，是否达到了那家公司的质量……？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Is this something that's going to customers, literally taste the soup. What's missing in it? I think at most companies that have a maniacally customer-focused founder, if you don't do that last step, it's going to be much more painful after you launch because they weren't part of that co-creation of the team. I think that formula winds up working pretty well if you throw in that alignment on principles and envision.
turns.zh: 这东西是要给客户的，得真的去尝那口汤。里面缺了什么？我觉得在大多数拥有『对客户着了魔般专注』的创始人的公司，如果你不做那最后一步，发布之后会痛苦得多，因为他们没参与团队那个共同创造的过程。我觉得，如果你把那个在原则上的对齐、以及愿景加进去，那个公式最终会相当管用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That usually sounds nice in theory, but I often imagine you get to that final step and the founder is like, "What the hell is this? This is not at all what I was hoping it be." Is there an example of that, that comes to mind where you maybe went through that and then it's just like, "No. That did not work out the way we expected" and if not, no problem.
turns.zh: 那通常在理论听起来挺好，但我常想象你到了那最后一步，创始人却像：『这他妈是什么？这完全不是我盼着的样子。』有没有一个这种例子，浮上你心头——也许你经历过那个，然后就：『不。那没按我们预期的那样成。』如果没有，也没关系。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. I mean I think that does happen. The ship is maybe ... the end of the year is the level of engagement and often that last level of engagement, that's where there's actually the most rapid refinement that you're doing. I think what's important there is that hopefully you're refining in code and you're not still at static design mocks because using the software is so different than looking at what the software will visually appear.
turns.zh: 对。我是说，我觉得那确实会发生。那艘船也许……年末是介入的程度，而往往那最后一级的介入，恰恰是你做最快速精修的地方。我觉得那里重要的是：希望你是在代码里精修，而不是还停在静态设计稿上，因为用这个软件和看这个软件视觉上会长什么样，是天差地别的。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think what we would wind up doing with Stewart at Slack, for example, is we would get the entire development team, engineers design product, user research and Stewart together in a room and we almost do a bug bash together. The idea was like, "We're doing it all together. We're trying to make the best product possible, making great softwares really messy and we're all trying to clean up the mess together."
turns.zh: 我觉得我们和 Stewart 在 Slack 会最终做的，比如，是把整个开发团队——工程师、设计、产品、用户研究——和 Stewart 一起请进一个房间，然后我们几乎像一起做个找虫大会。想法就像：『我们全在一起做。我们想造出尽可能最好的产品，造伟大的软件真的很乱，而我们都在试着一起把那摊乱收拾干净。』

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Sometimes you might find things like, "Okay. This entry point really isn't working, maybe we have to move this entry point. That's maybe a bigger change." But I think often what you'd find is just all those bits of polish and refinement and doing the little delightful things that might otherwise be missing to raise that craft bar and doing a real collective way so it doesn't just feel like the team says. "We want to ship." The founder says, "No, it's not ready."
turns.zh: 有时你可能会发现像：『好。这个入口点真的行不通，也许我们得挪这个入口点。那也许是更大的改动。』但我觉得你常会发现的是，就那些打磨和精修的碎片、以及做那些本可能被漏掉的小巧思，好把工艺的标杆抬上去，并且以一种真正集体的方式去做，这样它就不会只是感觉像团队说『我们想发。』创始人说『不，还没好。』

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Ideally as a group you're saying, We want to get it to a bar that's going to delight our users and here's the gap from where we are today to what we want to shift." I think that mentality winds up being a lot more constructive, but that's not always easy to do.
turns.zh: 理想地，作为一个群体你们在说：『我们想把它抬到一个能让我们用户惊艳的标杆，而这是从我们今天所在、到我们想移向之处之间的缺口。』我觉得那种心态最终会建设性得多，但那不总容易做到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about creating these principles, which is an awesome approach of just creating guardrails for the team so they think the way the founder and the head of product think. What are some examples of principles you have and had early on maybe at Foursquare or Slack?
turns.zh: 你聊到创立这些原则，这是一种很棒的做法——就给团队设护栏，好让他们按创始人和产品负责人思考的方式去想。你在早期——也许在 Foursquare 或 Slack——有过、并且拥有的一些原则例子是什么？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I mean Slack I think is where we enshrined them much more because we scaled the org so much, more that we needed principles. I think for us, they were really about unpacking just the mission, which for Slack is making people's working lives simpler, more pleasant, more productive. That's the mission of the company. The question is how does software help do that? That's what the principles or their answer.
turns.zh: 我是说，Slack 我觉得是我们把原则立得更牢的地方，因为我们组织扩张得那么多，更需要有原则。我觉得对我们来说，它们真正是关于拆解那个使命——对 Slack 而言，就是让人们的职业生活更简单、更愉快、更高产。那是公司的使命。问题是软件如何帮着做到那个？那正是那些原则、或者它们的答案。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: For us, we've got five, four principles. They've largely stayed the same. Some of the language has changed over the last couple of years. But at least for the last four or five years we've had these. The first is be a great host, which is all about that level of craft, the relentlessly saving people's steps. If you're, let's say, a host at Airbnb, it's like putting clean towels on the bed. No one has to wonder "Are these for me?" That type of foresight.
turns.zh: 对我们来说，我们有五条、四条原则。它们大体上没变。有些措辞在过去几年里改过。但至少过去四五年我们一直有这些。第一条是『做个好主人』，那全是关于那种工艺程度、那种不停地替人省步子。如果你，比如说，是 Airbnb 的一个房东，那就像在床上铺上干净的毛巾。没人会疑惑『这是给我的吗？』那类的先见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's actually a value at Airbnb. Exactly.
turns.zh: 那其实正是 Airbnb 的一个价值观。没错。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Oh, really?
turns.zh: 哦，真的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's actually be a host at Airbnb is one of the four core values.
turns.zh: 其实『在 Airbnb 做个主人』是四大核心价值之一。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Right. Maybe we borrowed that or someone was inspired by it. But be a great host. It sounded aspirational. I love that.
turns.zh: 对。也许我们借了那个，或者有人受它启发。但『做个好主人』。它听起来让人向往。我爱这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. It's a little bigger.
turns.zh: 对。对。它稍微大一点。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: There's a famous user design book called Don't Make Me Think, which we sold the title of for our next principle. That's really just about as people building the software, you know how it works so well. You care about all the nuances and intricacies and you really want your users to love it as much as you do. But often actually, that owner's delusion that someone else will care as much about the software that you built as you do, prevents you from actually making something that's simple, comprehensible, understandable.
turns.zh: 有本著名的用户设计书叫《别让我思考》，我们把它的书名拿来做我们下一条原则。那真的只是关于：作为造软件的人，你多懂它怎么运作得那么好。你在意所有的微妙和繁复，而你真的希望你的用户和你一样爱它。但往往，那种主人的错觉——以为别人会像你一样在乎你造的软件——反而阻止了你真正做出简单、可理解、看得懂的东西。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: One of the core tenets of Slack is pretty complex under the surface, is how do we actually make people not have to think, how do we not reinvent the wheel if there's existing design patterns to use, how do we actually wind up designing for people who come from many different backgrounds and we cater to their needs in ways that don't make them have to customize it too much?
turns.zh: Slack 的一条核心原则，表面下其实相当复杂，是：我们到底如何让人不必去想、如果有现成的设计范式可用，我们如何不去重复造轮子、我们到底如何为来自许多不同背景的人做设计，并以不让他们过度自定的方式去迎合他们的需求？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: There's a saying we also have, which is more clicks can often be okay. You'll often have in optimization experimentation circles like, "Oh, every click, remove it." But I actually think in a lot of software when it's not transactional, helping people understand what they're doing, giving them confidence, helping them have trust in the steps, we've seen that that can actually be a better experience. That's another example of don't make it stressful, help people chill out when they're using this offer. That's the idea beyond that one.
turns.zh: 我们还有一句说法，就是『多几次点击往往也行』。在优化实验圈子里，你常会听到像：『哦，每多一次点击，就去掉它。』但我其实觉得，在很多并非交易型的软件里，帮人理解他们在做什么、给他们信心、帮他们对那些步骤建立信任——我们见过，那其实可以是一种更好的体验。那是『别让它 stressful、帮人在用这个东西时放松下来』的另一个例子。那就是那一条背后的想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shifting a little bit. I know you guys have been working on a bunch of AI stuff at Slack. I believe you've been working on AI related stuff for many years. I think at Google you worked on a lot of AI related products. I feel like a lot of people are just getting into this and trying to figure out, "How do we integrate AI and ML and LLMs into our product and how do we not just waste our time chasing things?"
turns.zh: 稍微转个弯。我知道你们在 Slack 搞了一堆 AI 的东西。我相信你们搞 AI 相关的东西很多年了。我觉得在 Google 你做的是大量 AI 相关的产品。我感觉很多人刚入门，正试图搞清：『我们如何把 AI、ML 和 LLM 整合进我们的产品，又如何不只是浪费时间在追逐东西上？』

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to ask you just in your time working with AI over the many years you've been doing it and share a little bit about what you've been doing there. What are some things you've learned about how to be actually effective and build valuable products and not just fall for the shiny object issue and trap?
turns.zh: 我想问你，就在你这些年做 AI 的时光里，分享一点你在那儿做了什么。关于如何真正有效、造出有价值的产品、而不只是掉进闪亮物件的问题和陷阱里，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I mean, it's almost 15 years ago now that I was working at Google in search on what later became called the knowledge graph. This idea of building a canonical repository of information of people, places, things in the world and relationships between them. Back then, it was a lot of the same ideas, but obviously the techniques. I have got a lot more mature.
turns.zh: 我是说，差不多 15 年前了，我在 Google 搜索部门，做后来被称为知识图谱的东西。那个想法是建一个关于人、地点、事物、以及它们之间关系的、规范性的信息仓库。那时候，很多想法是一样的，但技术显然不同。现在的技术成熟得多。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: We used natural language processing to extract all this information from the web and try to build this database of facts. An idea then was could you take queries, people have like, "What are the tallest fountains in Europe or what of the most popular beaches in Southern California?" Be able to actually give answers not just 10 blue links.
turns.zh: 我们用自然语言处理，从网上抽取所有这些消息，试着建这个事实数据库。当时的一个想法是：你能否接住那些查询——人们会像：『欧洲最高的喷泉是哪些？或者南加州最受欢迎的海滩是哪些？』——从而真能给出答案，而不只是十个蓝色链接。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think the thing that's really changed, it's super exciting in the last 6, 12 months with LMs and chat GPT and everything else is the idea that now you can take not just knowledge about the world but actually have natural language generation where suddenly the computer can talk back to you in a way that feels extremely human. Then the creative applications of that are pretty massive and exciting.
turns.zh: 我觉得真正变了的东西，是在过去 6 到 12 个月里、随着 LM 和 ChatGPT 以及一切其他东西，超级令人兴奋的——那个想法是：如今你拿到的不只是关于世界的知识，而是真的有了自然语言生成，电脑突然能以极度像人的方式回你话。然后那带来的创造性应用，是相当庞大、也相当令人兴奋的。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: That's, I guess, the lineage there. I think from over the years back at Google at Foursquare, we did a lot of personalization and recommendations at Slack we have search and ML that's coming infused throughout the product. I think a couple things come out as ... I guess the principles that we've used over the years, back then at Google, one of the big ones, was that the promise of the UI has to match the quality of the underlying data, which is to say ... I think this is actually one of the failings of the various LMs right now is they all appear supremely confident even when they're completely hallucinating.
turns.zh: 那，我猜，就是那条血脉。我觉得从这些年——回 Google、在 Foursquare——我们在 Slack 做了大量个性化和推荐，我们有搜索和 ML 正被注入整个产品。我觉得有几件事浮现……我猜我们这些年里用的原则，当年在 Google，大的一条是：UI 的承诺必须匹配底层数据的质量，也就是说……我觉得这其实是当前各种 LM 的一个失败之处——它们哪怕在完全胡说八道时，也显得极度自信。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think that's going to be something that people are going to have to work on a lot, which is to figure out how to be not so faultless, to acknowledge when you're not sure, because otherwise, it undermines the trust people have in the system. Using a lot of transparency about where the data comes from so people can actually build credibility and the tools is really important.
turns.zh: 我觉得那会是人们将不得不大力去攻克的东西，也就是搞清如何别那么无懈可击，在你不确定时肯于承认，因为否则，它会破坏人们对系统的信任。大量运用关于数据从哪来的透明度，好让人们能真正建立起对工具和系统的可信度，是真的很重要。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Then I think making sure that as you're designing the products that you have virtuous cycles that are naturally part of the product experience where you can get training data as a byproduct of people naturally using the software and then can make the model that you're building behind the scenes smarter, more accurate, more predictive.
turns.zh: 然后我觉得，要确保在设计产品时，你有那些良性闭环，它们天然就是产品体验的一部分——你能把人们自然使用软件时产生的训练数据，当作副产品拿到，然后让背后那个你正在建的模型，变得更聪明、更准、更具预测力。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: A classic example of that would be Netflix back in the day, their rating system, they actually have a feedback loop from their customers then make the system better at predicting. I think people you are still trying to figure out what does that look like in this world in LLMs?
turns.zh: 一个经典的例子会是当年的 Netflix，他们的评分系统，其实有个来自客户的反馈回路，让系统更会预测。我觉得人们现在仍在试图搞清，在 LM 这个世界里，那会长什么样？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I hope that you're all building at Slack is a way to ask a bot questions based on all the conversations in the Slack. I've been looking for that product for a while now.
turns.zh: 有件东西，我希望你们在 Slack 都在建——一种基于 Slack 里所有对话、去问一个 bot 问题的方式。我找这种产品找了一阵子了。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I can safely say we have a lot of prototypes internally where we are playing with this. I think it is actually funny as a aside in one of the original Slack, I don't know, product vision decks back in 2014. There was our whole strategy, there's four parts. Then part number four, which was a joke at the time, was then do magic AI stuff on top.
turns.zh: 我可以安心地说，我们内部有大量的原型，正在玩这个。我觉得作为题外话其实很好笑：在最早的 Slack 里——我不知道——2014 年的产品愿景幻灯片里。我们有整套战略，分四部分。然后第四部分，当时是个玩笑，是『然后在上头做点神奇的 AI 东西』。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: We didn't even know what the state of AI would be. By the time hopefully companies have their collective knowledge in Slack and now we're finally at the period where the magic AI stuff seems finally pretty amazing, pretty magical. Yeah. We're doing a lot of prototyping internally and also trying to work with the ecosystem around as well, because there's so many companies doing amazing work in this space.
turns.zh: 我们当时根本不知道 AI 会是什么状态。等到（希望如此）各家公司把他们集体的知识放在 Slack 里，而如今我们终于到了那个阶段——神奇的 AI 东西似乎终于相当惊人、相当有魔力了。对。我们在内部做了大量原型，也在试图和周边的生态合作，因为有太多公司在这个空间里做着惊人的工作。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: That if you work at a company where you have so much knowledge in your Slack channel repository that you can suddenly get amazing leaps in productivity to help you better do your job because that knowledge is in Slack, but it's sometimes hard to reach and I think these technologies can make that possible.
turns.zh: 也就是，如果你在一家公司工作，而你的 Slack 频道仓库里有那么多知识，你能突然获得惊人的生产力跃升，帮自己把工作做得更好——因为那知识在 Slack 里，但有时很难够到——而我觉得这些技术能让那成为可能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of something Gustav, the CPO and CTO and co-president of Spotify share that they always have a deck and a vision of just a play button within Spotify, you just play and all magic happens and it's the best music and thing exactly what you want to hear and just how that isn't actually possible and it's still not possible. Exactly to your point, you have to really think about how does it act? How close is it to the reality? If it's not actually there, he was saying how like, "We'll pick two songs that are correct at a 10 just because we don't really know exactly what you want to hear right now."
turns.zh: 这让我想起 Gustav——Spotify 的 CPO 兼 CTO 兼联席总裁——分享过的一件事：他们总有一份幻灯片和一个愿景，就是在 Spotify 里只要一个播放键，你一按，所有魔法就发生，放出正合你意、最棒的音乐。而那其实不可能，而且至今仍不可能。正合你的点，你得真的去想：它实际表现如何？它离现实多近？如果它其实不在那儿，他当时就说，像：『我们就挑两首对的歌，准确率大概 10 吧，因为我们其实并不确切知道你现在想听什么。』

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's no point in trying to design that right now because that's not actually going to be delivering on the promise.
turns.zh: 现在去设计那个没意义，因为它其实交付不了那个承诺。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Right. Yeah. I love that. Our version of that has always been that you open up Slack and suddenly instead of having to read through dozens of channels or find these mentions that magically Slack could just tell you in order that you would care about a summary of all the interesting things that have happened and then let you dig in if you want to your very own personal chief of staff who knew everything that you cared about and read everything that you could read.
turns.zh: 对。对。我爱那个。我们那个的版本，一直是：你打开 Slack，突然间，不必再去翻几十条频道、或者找那些 @提及，Slack 能神奇地、按你会在意的方式，直接告诉你一个所有发生过的、有意思之事的摘要，然后如果你想深挖，它让你挖——就像你专属的、私人参谋长，知道你在意的一切、也读完了你能读的一切。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I don't think that's going to quite be possible anytime soon. But I think Spotify heading towards that north star you wind up developing. I hope a lot of really compelling projects experiences along the way.
turns.zh: 我觉得那短期内还不太可能完全成真。但我觉得到那个北极星，Spotify 正在行进而去，你最终会发育出它。我希望沿途有一大堆真正引人入胜的项目体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, man. The more I think about it, the more amazing opportunities exist in Slack. It's all text. It's amazing. Okay. There's a lot of cool stuff coming I imagine.
turns.zh: 对，老兄。我越想，Slack 里存在的惊人机会就越多。它全是文字。太惊人了。好。我想象有一大堆酷东西要来。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can't wait.
turns.zh: 我等不及了。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On that topic, how do you think about creating teams within Slack and AI specifically? Are you recommending each team think about how AI can make their stuff better or are you dedicating, "Here's the AI team and they're going to work on stuff" and you guys just keep ship what you're shipping and keep moving your metrics?
turns.zh: 顺着那个话题，你是怎么思考在 Slack 内、specifically 在 AI 上组建团队的？你是在建议每个团队都想想『AI 如何让我们自己的东西更好』，还是你在专设：『这是 AI 团队，他们去搞东西』，而你们就继续发你们在发的、继续推动你们的指标？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I mean the unfair answer is a hybrid of the two, which is to say we have a central machine learning and search team. But a lot of people have expertise in this field to build infrastructure that everybody can use. What we've done is because the space is evolving so quickly, literally every month, the capabilities are evolving, the risks and tradeoffs are evolving a ton.
turns.zh: 我是说，不偏不倚的答案是两者的混合——也就是，我们有一个中央的机器学习与搜索团队。但很多人有这个领域的专长，能建出人人可用的基础设施。我们所做的，是因为这个空间演进得太快了，literally 每个月，能力在演进、风险和权衡也在大量演进。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: What we want to do is actually spin up a couple different teams that are focused on prototyping, using that common infrastructure but in specific directions that are all a little bit different. We've got a common ML, let's say in search team and now we have a bunch of teams that are working in parallel and different customer problems that we're trying to solve using that shared infrastructure.
turns.zh: 我们想做的，其实是启动几个不同的团队，专注于原型开发，用那套共同的基础设施，但朝各自略有不同、特定的方向。我们有个共同的 ML——比如说在搜索团队——而如今我们有一批团队，在平行地、针对不同客户问题工作，试图用那套共享基础设施去解决。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think this isn't the steady state. I think over time, what it'll probably look like is that all the existing product areas, as soon as we know more of the shape of what the technology is capable of will just have AI capabilities as part of their roadmaps. Just like every product team is responsible for their own mobile roadmap. They don't outsource it to someone else.
turns.zh: 我觉得这不是稳态。我觉得随着时间，它大概会长成这样：所有既有的产品板块，一旦我们对技术能成什么样的轮廓知道更多，就会把 AI 能力作为它们路线图的一部分。就像每个产品团队都对自家的移动路线图负责。他们不会把它外包给别人。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But I think today when things are moving so quickly, you actually want a little bit of a more ad hoc, flexible approach to move quickly and that's what we're doing.
turns.zh: 但我觉得到今天，当事情动得这么快，你其实想要一种更临机、更灵活的做法去快速移动——而那正是我们在做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's what I've been hearing from everyone I've been asking this question. The search ranking team is always seems to be the center of all this and then it's a few experiments here and there. That's an interesting pattern I've been noticing.
turns.zh: 那正是我问过这问题的人里，大家都告诉我的。搜索排序团队似乎总是这一切的中心，然后这儿那儿有几个实验。那是我注意到的一个有趣模式。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Good to know.
turns.zh: 知道了就好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I heard that you have a process internally called Complaint-Storms. I'd love to understand what that is.
turns.zh: 我听说你们内部有个流程叫『抱怨风暴』（Complaint-Storms）。我很想弄懂那是什么。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: It something that started. I want to say back in end of 2019, maybe early 2020. The idea a little bit was how do we help as a team look at the software that we build with fresh eyes, because we've been set at Slack for a long time. Slack maybe more than almost any other company maybe like Figma is probably similar. I was listening to the podcast just earlier today where if you work on Figma, you work on Slack.
turns.zh: 那是很久前开始的东西。我想说是 2019 年底、也许 2020 年初。那个想法有点是：作为团队，我们如何带着新鲜的眼睛，去看我们造的软件——因为我们在 Slack 待太久了。Slack 也许比几乎任何别的公司都更甚，也许像 Figma 大概也类似。我今天稍早就在听那个播客，里面说如果你在 Figma 工作，你就在 Slack 工作。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: You also live in Slack and you live in Figma all day so you can become more of a power user than anyone else on earth. What we were realizing, especially for people trying to build Slack for the next million customers, the people who have never used Slack before, it was becoming increasingly hard to have empathy for what their usage of Slack would look like. How would they look at it in a more critical way? How would they care less than we cared?
turns.zh: 你也整天活在 Slack 里、活在 Figma 里，于是你能成为比地球上任何人都更强的超级用户。我们当时意识到，尤其对那些试图为下一批百万客户建 Slack 的人——那些从没用过 Slack 的人——要去共情他们的 Slack 用法会长什么样，正变得愈来愈难。他们会以更挑剔的方式看它吗？他们会比我们在意得少吗？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: What we started doing with these complaints storms and idea was really simple, which is we'd get a team together often Stewart myself would also join and we'd actually start off with other products first in adjacent spaces and we'd say, "Okay. As a group we're going to go through the customer journey from the moment you land on the website through, let's say it's a workplace product, getting your first account going, getting the first couple of users on board, getting to the point of value.
turns.zh: 我们开始做这些抱怨风暴，想法其实很简单：我们会把团队聚起来——常常 Stewart 和我自己也会加入——而我们会真的先从相邻空间里别的产品开始，然后我们说：『好。作为一个群体，我们要走一遍客户旅程——从你踏上网站的那一刻起，穿过——比如说那是个职场产品——开起你的第一个账户、让头几个用户上船、走到价值点。』

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: We're going to do it on one screen. Someone's going to project and then people are going to fill in every issue, everything that's confusing, every pain point, not bones, but ways in which if you didn't care about the software, you don't work on it, what would actually confuse you? What would stop you in your tracks?
turns.zh: 我们要在一块屏幕上做。有人会投屏，然后人们会填进每一个问题、每样让人困惑的东西、每一个痛点——不是骨头，而是：如果你不在乎这软件、你不在它上工作，什么会真的让你困惑？什么会让你当场愣住？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: From that you went generating a bunch of amazing inspiration by looking at someone else's product in a really critical way for things you might want to try in your own product. Once you get to that, then it becomes easier to actually do with your own software, but it is a little painful obviously. Same with watching usability tests to look at your own baby in a way that is, "Okay. I'm trying to find all the words. I'm trying to find all the problems."
turns.zh: 从那个出发，你通过用真正挑剔的方式看别人的产品，生出了大量惊人的灵感，针对你也许想在自己产品里试的东西。一旦你到了那一步，再去对自己家的软件做，就更容易了——但它显然有点痛。看可用性测试、以『好，我在试图找出所有的词、找出所有的问题』的方式去看自家的孩子，也是同理。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But that's one up being a pretty great source. Whenever a team I think either gets stuck or feels like they reach a dead end in a direction is doing complaint-storms about the product area that they're in or using adjacent products just to get inspiration. Then I think it unlocks a lot more creative views than the problem space.
turns.zh: 但那最终成了相当棒的源头。我觉得，无论何时一个团队卡住、或者觉得自己在一个方向上走到了死胡同，去做针对他们所在产品板块的抱怨风暴、或者用相邻产品，就只是为了拿灵感。然后我觉得，它解锁的创造性视角，远比问题空间本身多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's similar to a process that I learned Stripe has called friction logging. But I love the nuance here of starting with someone else's product because I could totally see how that makes you feel better looking at your product in real life. It's not like we suck. It's okay, everyone's has so much opportunity.
turns.zh: 它类似于我得知 Stripe 有个叫『摩擦记录』的流程。但我爱这里那个微妙处——从别人的产品开始——因为我完全能看出，那如何让你在真实生活里看自家产品时感觉更好。不是像『我们烂』。而是：好，人人都还有那么多机会。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah. I've heard that from Stripe, too. I think gets a similar place. I think it's the doing it ... I think the byproduct is that you also get calibration on product pace, product quality, and as a team you develop that together. Again, similar to the principles, it's like how do you get these things that are hard to actually feel collectively on the same page about and how do you calibrate? It's another good way to do it.
turns.zh: 没错。对。这个我也从 Stripe 听过。我觉得它到的是相似的地方。我觉得做这件事……我觉得那个副产品是：你也在产品节奏、产品质量上拿到了校准，而且作为一个团队，你们一起把它发展出来。再说一次，类似于那些原则，它就像：你如何让这些难在集体上真正同页共感的东西被感觉到、并且你如何校准？那是另一种好做法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm imagining some PMs might be hearing this and wonder, "Okay. Great. Now the founders and the execs have all these things that they want us to fix. I have goals to hit. I got a roadmap. How do you think about prioritizing things that come up in these sorts of sessions for the team and how do they mix and match versus all the other stuff that you want to do? Or is it just like they don't actually have a huge roadmap and this is a way to inform the roadmap?
turns.zh: 我在想象，有些 PM 也许正听着这个、然后纳闷：『好。棒。现在创始人和高管有了所有这些他们想让我们修的东西。我有要达成的目标。我有路线图。你是怎么思考、为团队排定这些在那种会议里冒出来的东西的优先级？它们和你所有其他想做的事，如何混搭？还是说，其实他们并没有一张巨大的路线图，而这只是个给路线图提供信息的方式？』

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: No. I mean, more broadly, I think the way that we think about, or us to think about our roadmap for any feature team at Slack is that it's a portfolio and it's meant to be a portfolio that's diversified a couple different ways. I think one is you want to diversify things that are meant to be new capabilities versus making the thing you've already built a little bit better every day. Similar to parenting.
turns.zh: 不。我是说，往宽里讲，我觉得我们思考的方式——或者我们在 Slack 对任何功能团队的路线图去思考的方式——是把它当成一份组合，而且它该是一份以几种不同方式做了多元化的组合。我觉得其一，你想让意在成为新能力的、和每天把你已造出的东西弄好一点点的，做多元化。类似于育儿。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Are there things that are meant to be risky that you aren't sure are going to work but might have a lot of upside versus things that are known bets. Then I think often you're balancing are you doing things that are meant to have impact that you're already very confident in versus things that are meant to learn about a new possibility space.
turns.zh: 有没有那种意在冒险、你不确定会成、却可能有大量上行的东西，相对地，有没有那种已知的下注？然后我觉得，你常是在平衡：你做的是意在产生你已经很有把握的影响的东西，还是意在了解一个新可能性空间的东西？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think for most teams, this stuff usually wind up tactically filling up that bucket of, "Let's make the existing product a little bit better every day for users." At Slack we have this thing we call customer Love Sprints, which is an interesting way team to figure out how to get this on their roadmap is it's hard to allocate that work throughout the quarter.
turns.zh: 我觉得对大多数团队，这类事往往最终在战术上填进了那个桶：让我们每天给用户把既有产品弄好一点点。在 Slack 我们有个叫客户热爱冲刺的东西，它是个有意思的方式——团队能搞清如何把这件事放上自己的路线图，因为要在整个季度里拨出那块工作，很难。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: What we'll wind up doing often is have a team do a two-week customer love sprint, almost like a hackathon, but with that burndown list of what we think is the lowest effort, highest impact changes that we can make to generate more love from our customers and whatever that feature areas. Then people just sprint for two weeks, design product engineering, and then you have a bunch of things that you celebrate.
turns.zh: 我们最终常做的，是让一个团队做一个为期两周的客户热爱冲刺，简直像个黑客松，但带着那样一张燃尽表——列着我们觉得是最低投入、最高影响的改动，能给我们的客户生出更多热爱、无论在那哪个功能板块。然后人们就冲刺两周，设计、产品、工程，然后你就有一大堆值得庆祝的东西。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: At the end, the goal is to ship all of them. This isn't hacks that you throw away. That's how we end up prioritizing it off in that work is actually making it this really fun total change of pace throughout the quarter to not do big feature work that may take months, but to do all these small delightful things that customers are going to love at the end. That's the other way that we figure out how to balance it in.
turns.zh: 到末尾，目标是把它们全发出来。这不是你扔掉的那些 hack。那是我们最终如何在那块工作里排定优先级——它其实让整个季度有了一种真正好玩的、彻底的节奏变化：不去做大块可能要花几个月的功能工作，而是去做所有这些小的、客户最终会热爱的巧思。那是我们搞清如何平衡它的另一种方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. How often do you do these sorts of customer Love Sprints?
turns.zh: 我爱这个。你们多常做这种客户热爱冲刺？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I would think teams that work on very user facing products do it at least once a quarter. I think other teams that work on maybe less user facing might do it maybe twice a year. But quarterly is a pretty healthy cadence.
turns.zh: 我会想，做非常直面用户产品的团队，至少每季度做一次。我觉得别的、也许没那么直面用户的团队，也许一年两次。但每季度是个相当健康的节奏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I didn't know about that. That connects to ... Slack has always been a very delightful product. I remember early on the animations were so awesome, the little twirly, I don't know, pounds hashtag thing. It feels like Slack has always invested in delight. How do you operationalize that? Is it these customer Love Sprints? Is there something else that's just like we need to allocate some percentage, just make things really fun even though it's not going to move any metric?
turns.zh: 哇。我之前不知道这个。这连上了……Slack 一直是个让人很愉悦的产品。我记得早期那些动画超棒，那个小转转、我不知道、pounds 的井号东西。感觉 Slack 一直都在愉悦上下注。你们如何把它运营化？是靠这些客户热爱冲刺吗？还是有别的，就像：我们得拨出某个百分比，就为了让东西真的好玩，哪怕它不会推动任何指标？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I would say it's a little bit good DNA of the company, honestly, which is that for co-founders trying to build a massive online role playing game for many years that was called Glitch and their background was all in building delightful, playful experiences. Glitch didn't work out. But, yeah, there's a whole long backstory. But the short version is a tool they had built internally that they then wound up spitting out a company from which became Slack.
turns.zh: 我会说，老实讲，那是公司一点点好的 DNA——也就是那几位联合创始人，曾花很多年试图建一个庞大的在线角色扮演游戏，叫 Glitch，而他们的背景全在打造愉悦的、好玩的体验。Glitch 没成。但，对，有一整个长长的背景故事。简短版是：他们内部建过一个工具，然后那个工具最终吐出了一家公司，而那家公司成了 Slack。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think that DNA we're trying to build a consumer grade experience that just happens to be for work is really ingrained in the company. It's also a big part of how we hire. I would say certainly the majority of PMs designers and engineers who joined Slack had never worked at an enterprise software company before. It's not like most people had worked at Oracle or SAP, it's most people had worked at consumer companies or game companies.
turns.zh: 我觉得那个 DNA——我们试图打造一种恰好是用在职场上的消费级体验——是真的深植于公司的。它也是我们如何招人的一大块。我会说，确实，加入 Slack 的大多数 PM、设计师和工程师，之前从没在一家企业软件公司干过。不像大多数人在 Oracle 或 SAP 干过，大多数人在消费级公司或游戏公司干过。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: They bring that focus in the spirit and then I would say the last bit beyond kind of the principles and the complaints-storms and the customer love is that we have this amazing team that we call the CET team, the Customer Experience Team. They're in some ways the team that is doing our scale at Foursquare is most often in touch with our customers.
turns.zh: 他们把那种专注带进精神里，然后我会说，除了那些原则、抱怨风暴、和客户热爱之外，最后一块是：我们有个超棒的团队，叫 CET 团队，也就是客户体验团队。在某种程度上，他们是在规模上——就像我们在 Foursquare 时——最常和我们的客户接触的团队。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: From the very early days people used to do CE shifts if you worked in products so that you can actually figure out what's frustrating, what's confusing. We have a really great pipeline for getting the insights from the CE team of what are the obstacles, the pain points, the most frequent complaints into the hands of the product teams to be able to prioritize, to figure out, yeah, not all these are going to move a given metric. They might not achieve something for the business.
turns.zh: 从很早的日子起，如果你在产品部门工作，人们会去做 CE 轮值，好让你真能搞清什么让人沮丧、什么让人困惑。我们有一个真的很棒的管线，能把来自 CE 团队的洞察——哪些是障碍、哪些是痛点、哪些是最频繁的抱怨——交到产品团队手里，让他们能排定优先级、能搞清：对，不是所有这些都会推动某个给定指标。它们也许不会为公司达成什么。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But collectively, I think the way that Slack thinks about competition is we obsess it about customers. We build something they'll love enough to tell their coworkers and the rest takes care of itself.
turns.zh: 但集合起来，我觉得 Slack 思考竞争的方式是：我们对客户着了魔。我们造出某种东西，让他们爱到会去告诉同事，其余的自会照料自己。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of competition, something I wanted to ask you a bit about. Early on Slack was competing against this product called HipChat and that's actually what I used at our startup and we love HipChat. It was so hilarious, just these memes everywhere and their billboards are amazing. But then Slack ate their lunch later on. I'm just thinking out loud, discord feels like that was the big threat and how Microsoft Teams obviously.
turns.zh: 说到竞争，有件事我想稍微问你一下。早期 Slack 在和一款叫 HipChat 的产品竞争，那其实正是我们创业公司用的，我们超爱 HipChat。它那么好笑，到处都是那些梗图，他们的广告牌也惊人。但后来 Slack 把他们的午餐吃掉了。我只是在大声想，Discord 感觉像是那个大威胁，还有显然的 Microsoft Teams。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious just how you think about competition and even just what you've learned about working in a space where there's a lot of competition and thinking about that long-term and even short-term.
turns.zh: 我纯粹好奇你是怎么思考竞争的，还有就在个竞争很强的空间里工作你学到了什么，以及关于那个的长期、甚至短期思考。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. I mean each of those is an interesting mini lesson learned about those. I think the through line for all of them I would say is still the max that we have in trailing, which is we're customer obsessed but competitor aware. I think it's a little bit different. I think some companies are like ... I don't know, Uber for example, I think was notorious competitor obsessed and they tried to delete customers when they could.
turns.zh: 对。我是说，它们每一个都是关于那些、学到的一个有趣的小教训。我觉得贯穿它们全体的那根线，我会说是我们一直拽在手里的最大原则，也就是：我们对客户着了魔，但对竞争对手有意识。我觉得这有点不一样。我觉得有些公司像……我不知道，比如 Uber，我觉得是出了名的对竞争对手着了魔，而且一有机会就想干掉客户。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think HipChat. I don't think Slack sought out to kill HipChat. At Foursquare we used ... I think it was called Campfire back in the day for the 37 singles people. It was a whole generation of those products. I think Slack came along and I think they had a couple of innovations. One was they had a great mobile experience that synced across every client. Search actually worked and then they brought a lot of the best parts of consumer messaging into the workplace like the emoji and reactions and all those bits.
turns.zh: 我觉得 HipChat。我不觉得 Slack 是处心积虑要干掉 HipChat 的。在 Foursquare 我们用过……我记得当年叫 Campfire，给那 37 个单身的哥们用。那是整整一代的这类产品。我觉得 Slack 后来居上，而我觉得他们有几项创新。其一，他们有个很棒的、能跨每个客户端同步的移动体验。搜索是真的能用，然后他们把消费级通讯里最好的那些部分——比如 emoji 和表情回应、以及所有那些碎片——带进了职场。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think it turns out that if you're 10X better on a couple of those axes, then you can see a huge change in behavior. I think that's what happened with that move from the HipChat Campfire to Slack world. Discords interesting. I mean we keep aware of Discord. But it is so much more focused on the consumer. Originally, it was [inaudible 00:36:23] out for community space. I think at Slack the lesson I would have, I think we learned in a good way is we've always really been focused on groups of people who are trying to do work together.
turns.zh: 我觉得结果证明，如果你在那几个轴向上好出 10 倍，你就能看到行为的巨大改变。我觉得那就是从 HipChat、Campfire 世界转向 Slack 世界时发生的事。Discord 有意思。我是说我们一直对 Discord 有意识。但它那么地更聚焦在消费级。最初，它是为社区空间而生的。我觉得在 Slack，我会给的教训是——我觉得我们以好的方式学到了——我们一直真的聚焦在正试图一起把工作做出来的一群人上。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: That winds up being a completely different audience to build for than communities. I think that focus has been really helpful and I think Discord's amazing and many people love it and the people who use Discord certainly use it in very different way than people who use Slack at work.
turns.zh: 那最终成了和社区完全不同的、要去构建的受众。我觉得那个聚焦一直很有帮助，而且我觉得 Discord 很惊人、很多人爱它，而用 Discord 的人，用法肯定和在工作里用 Slack 的人非常不同。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think Microsoft obviously has become over time the biggest competitor there. I think the origin of Teams really was a defensive move for them to protect Office because Office is an incredible, very profitable monopoly in the productivity space. I think when they built Teams it was more of a covering their flank versus Slack on the ascent.
turns.zh: 我觉得 Microsoft 显然随着时间成了那里最大的竞争对手。我觉得 Teams 的起源，对他们来说真的是一步防守棋，用来保护 Office，因为 Office 是生产力空间里一个不可思议、极赚钱的垄断。我觉得他们建 Teams 时，更多是在掩护自己的侧翼，相对当时正在上升的 Slack。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think as Teams has evolved over time, it's become much more of a video conferencing product that competes with Zoom and Google Meet. The people who use Teams use it completely different than Slack where you live and breathe and channels and work and workflows all day long.
turns.zh: 我觉得随着 Teams 随时间演进，它成了更偏视频会议的产品，和 Zoom、Google Meet 竞争。用 Teams 的人，用法和用 Slack 的人完全不同——在 Slack 里你整天活着、呼吸着、频道、工作、工作流。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think what we've seen there too is that a lot of our customers, they happily use both. Most Fortune 500 companies have either a subscription or a Google Workplace subscription and all of those customers who use those also use Slack. We like to say that Slack is this connected tissue that makes all the rest of your tools that much better.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们在那儿也看到的是：我们很多客户，都开心地两个都用。大多数财富 500 强公司，要么有 Slack 订阅、要么有 Google Workplace 订阅，而所有那些用那些的客户，也都用 Slack。我们喜欢说：Slack 是那块相连的组织，让其余所有你的工具都变好那么多。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think there we've taken very much an open ecosystem and platform approach and we've just been focused on how do we keep building the best version of what Slack can be as a new category of software for our customers and staying aware of our competitors, but really obsessed on what are the new ways that we can delight our users as the years go by.
turns.zh: 我觉得在那儿，我们采取的是非常开放的生态和平台路线，而我们一直聚焦在：作为软件的一个新品类，我们如何持续造出 Slack 能成为的最好版本，给我们的客户；并且对竞争对手保持有意识，但真的对客户着了魔——关于随着年岁流去，我们有哪些新方式能让我们用户惊艳。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Slack is a big-ish company within now let's say a big company. But it feels like you still are launching really interesting stuff, you launch huddles, clips, there's this AI stuff coming, sounds like. I'm curious what you have done at Slack to enable these sorts of zero to one bets and what you've seen is important to allow for innovation along those lines.
turns.zh: Slack 如今就算是个挺大的公司、可以说大公司了。但感觉你们仍在发布真正有意思的东西，你们发 huddles、clips，还有这听起来要来的 AI 东西。我好奇，你在 Slack 做了什么，去促成这类从零到一的下注，以及你看到什么对沿这些线的创新是重要的。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think maybe we're all a little self-delusional, because I think everyone who works at Slack likes to think that we're still at a small startup. I think keeping that spirit alive, honestly culturally has been a big part of it. I think going back to the principles early on, one of the ones that we did talk about, literally one of the actual wording is take bigger boulder bets.
turns.zh: 我觉得也许我们全都有点自我妄想，因为我觉得每个在 Slack 工作的人都喜欢觉得自己还在一个小创业公司。我觉得老实讲，在文化上让那种精神活着，一直是其中一大块。我觉得回到早期那些原则，我们确实聊过的其中之一，字面上一句确切的说法就是：下更大胆的赌注。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: The idea there is that it's really easy to fall into the trap of just constant incrementalism. The concept, it's like a feature team and you have like a KPI and you feel like your whole life is measured by that similar KPI going up 1% a quarter and then you lose sight of what's beyond the horizon. We have this mental metaphor that we talk a lot about getting to the next hill.
turns.zh: 那个想法是：跌进只是不停渐进的陷阱，真的很容易。那个概念，就像一个有功能的团队，你有个 KPI，而你觉得自己的整段人生都被那个类似的 KPI 每季度涨 1% 衡量着，然后你就看不见地平线之外是什么了。我们有这个常聊的心智隐喻：爬到下一座山头。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: The idea is that if you're in a mountain range and you're maybe in the little valley, you can see what's right in front of you. But you have no idea how tall the mountains are behind. I think teams can often get lost crawling up that hill, not realizing that there's a huge, incredibly beautiful range behind it.
turns.zh: 那个想法是：如果你在一道山脉里、也许在那个小山谷里，你能看到正眼前的是什么。但你根本不知道背后那些山有多高。我觉得团队常常会在爬那座山时迷失，没意识到它背后还有一片巨大、美得惊人的山脉。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Take bigger boulder bets. Get to the next hill to see what the horizon wants around you. That's how we think about it strategically. Then I think structurally the way we've approached it is that we've over time freighted new teams from scratch that incubated in a new area before the area mature. We did that with a lot of these native audiovisual products like huddles and clips really in the pandemic because our customers were demanding it from us.
turns.zh: 下更大胆的赌注。爬到下一座山头，去看看你周遭的地平线想要什么。那就是我们从战略上思考它的方式。然后我觉得，在结构上我们切入它的方式是：随着时间，我们从零组建了新的团队，让它们在某个领域成熟之前，在新区里孵化。我们在大流行期间，就是针对一大批这类原生的影音产品——比如 huddles 和 clips——这么做的，因为我们的客户在向我们强烈要求。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: They were like, "We love living in Slack all day. But we feel disconnected from our teammates when we can't be in the same physical place. What can you do to help us?" That's where that came from. I think in the AI space now, it's a similar thing, which is what we're trying to hear from customers. What do you wish Slack could do if it had these new superpowers? Let's incubate a couple teams, a prototype there and then figure out what can get to real product market fit.
turns.zh: 他们当时像：我们爱整天活在 Slack 里。但当我们没法在同一个实体场所时，我们觉得和队友失联了。你能做什么帮我们？那就是它从哪儿来的。我觉得如今在 AI 空间，是类似的事，也就是我们在试着听客户的声音。如果 Slack 有了这些新超能力，你希望它能做什么？我们孵化几个团队、在那儿做个原型，然后搞清什么能走到真正的产品市场契合。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think when we have those teams, I think it's important to just give them space to run, to give them ... get a gel free card for maybe the normal process of, "Okay. Our planning quarterly reviews" and make it feel something that is the pace of learning is what matters. How fast are you prototyping, how fast are you learning from users and then getting to do that publicly and pilot and then get something to launch that's amazing, blows people away. That's the formula that we've seen.
turns.zh: 我觉得当我们有了那些团队，重要的是就给他们空间去跑、给他们一张免凝胶卡，也许免去那个常规流程：好。我们的计划、季度评审，并且让它感觉：真正要紧的是学习的节奏。你原型做得有多快、你从用户那儿学得有多快，然后得以公开地做、去试点，然后做出一个能发布、能惊艳众人的东西。那就是我们见过的公式。
