turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the things I love learning about from product teams is their unique rituals and traditions. I'm curious what's maybe the most interesting or unique or fun or funny ritual or tradition on the product team of things you all maybe do regularly?
turns.zh: 我从产品团队那儿最爱学的一件事，就是他们独特的仪式和传统。我好奇，在你们产品团队里，也许最有趣、最独特、最好玩或最好笑的仪式或传统是什么，也许是你们定期会做的？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: One of the things that we do, which is always a little bit funny, I mean, it's more of a emotional thing rather than a practical thing is that at all hands we'll often wind up taking specific tweets that people had about the product and Twitter. People say the craziest thing sometimes. Sometimes they're really heartwarming like customer love, but often it's just the meanest, most frustrating complaints that people have.
turns.zh: 我们做的一件事，一直有点好笑——我是说，它更多是情绪性的、而非实用性的——是在全员大会上，我们常会搬出一些特定的、人们对产品和 Twitter 发的推文。人们有时会说最疯的话。有时它们真的暖心，像客户的热爱，但往往那只是人们最刻薄、最让人沮丧的抱怨。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: It's honestly meant for us to just have a pulse on, we're at people actually saying and feeling in the wild and not thinking too seriously, but keeping that sense of ... I think that the distance you have from your users as your user base gets more and more diverse and larger I think can make it harder to actually develop the product because you're not designing for yourself anymore.
turns.zh: 它老实讲是为了让我们自己有个脉搏：在野地里，人们到底在说什么、感受什么，而不必太严肃地想，但保持着那种感觉……我觉得，随着你的用户群变得愈来愈多元、愈来愈大，你和用户之间的距离，反而会让真正去开发产品变得更难，因为你不再是在为自己设计了。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think all the ways that we help keep people grounded in what are actual users actually saying. That's one big way. The other that reminded me of which is actually probably better, maybe delete that last one because it's kind of boring.
turns.zh: 我觉得所有那些我们帮着让人们扎根在真实用户到底在说什么上的方式。那是一个大方式。另一个让我想起的——其实也许更好——也许是删掉上一条，因为它有点无聊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No. It's great. We're not deleting nothing.
turns.zh: 不。它很棒。我们什么都不会删。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Fine. Usability. I'm a big believer in you want to be data-informed, but you don't want to be so data-driven that you actually don't have a pulse of what real people feel when they're using your product. We're really big into user research, not as it gives you the answer, but it helps at least pose a lot of questions for you when you watch how someone actually uses the software.
turns.zh: 行。可用性。我是个大信徒：你想被数据告知，但你不想被数据驱动到——当你其实对用户在用你产品时的真实感受，完全没有脉搏。我们超投入用户研究，不是因为它给你答案，而是当你看一个人到底怎么用这个软件时，它至少帮着你提出大量问题。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Historically, it's really hard to get PMs, let alone engineers actually attend user research sessions. What we wound up doing, especially in the pandemic when we first went remote, is now you can dial into usability sessions and to make it really attractive for the team, what we would do is have people live in a thread, write their real time thoughts of ... so painful, how they use that, or I can't believe they missed that, or, oh, that gave me this idea from seeing how they were doing that to do this other thing.
turns.zh: 历史上，要让 PM 们——更别提工程师——真的去参加用户研究环节，真的很难。我们最终做的，尤其在我们最初转远程、在大流行期间，是如今你能拨进可用性环节；而为了让它对团队真正有吸引力，我们做的是：让人们活在一个 thread 里，写下他们实时的想法——比如那么痛、他们怎么用那个、或者我真不敢信他们漏掉了那个、或者哦那个给了我这个点子、从看他们怎么做那个、去做另一个东西。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Then you wind up having the PMs, the engineers, designers and the user researcher all in one Slack thread live, responding, reacting to usability session. Then suddenly that thread becomes actually the best source of truth for the research report that then gets written up.
turns.zh: 然后你最终让 PM、工程师、设计师和用户研究员，全在一个 Slack thread 里、实时地，回应、对可用性环节做出反应。然后突然间，那个 thread 其实成了那篇研究报告的、最好的真相源头，而报告随后会被写就。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But I think most importantly, it gets the team almost like the complaint-storms, but actually watching someone else do it in the shoes of an actual human being trying to use the thing that you thought was so brilliant and yet has all these flaws. It's humbling. It's filled with humor and also it's I think really constructive for the teams to do it that way.
turns.zh: 但我觉得最重要的，是它让团队——几乎像抱怨风暴那样——但其实是看着另一个人，穿着一个真实人类、试图用那个你本以为那么 brilliant、却有着所有这些缺陷的东西的鞋。那是让人谦卑的。它充满幽默，而且我觉得，对团队以那种方式去做，真的很有建设性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to ask where they actually share these thoughts. In Slack makes a lot of sense.
turns.zh: 我正要问，他们到底在哪儿分享这些想法。在 Slack 里分享，很说得通。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. I mean it turns into a report at some point, but literally just link back to the original thread and then you have 100 people's reaction as the report is ongoing.
turns.zh: 对。我是说它到某个点会变成一份报告，但 literally 只要链回那个原始 thread，然后你就有 100 个人的反应，而报告还在进行中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If only there was a AI tool to summarize all of your thoughts.
turns.zh: 要是有一个 AI 工具能帮你把脑子里那些想法全都总结一下就好了。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: We've got a prototype for that. Hopefully it'll work well enough that actually be useful for customers, too.
turns.zh: 我们已经做了一个原型。希望它真的够好用，不仅对我们有用，对客户也能真正派上用场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You tweeted once about how ... I think maybe around the time you joined Slack around 2019 that the self-service business of Slack basically plateaued and it wasn't clear why. I'm curious just what that period was like and how did you get to the bottom of what was going on and turn things around.
turns.zh: 你曾经发过一条推文，大概是在 2019 年你加入 Slack 前后，说 Slack 的自助服务业务基本停滞了，而且搞不清楚原因。我很好奇那段时期到底是什么样子的，你是怎么弄清楚到底发生了什么，又是怎么扭转局面的。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. It was actually a couple years after I joined, but it was a point where I was focused on the self-service business because we had this period with Slack where I would say maybe 2014 to 2017 where it was almost all self-service and it was just growing like gangbusters. Then we started spinning up the sales team and an enterprise team. We started focusing mostly on that.
turns.zh: 对。其实那是我加入几年之后的事了，但当时我正专注于自助服务业务。因为 Slack 有过一段时期，大概从 2014 到 2017 年，几乎全都是自助服务，而且增长得极其疯狂。后来我们开始组建销售团队和企业团队，重心就主要转向了那边。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think we saw the team that was working on, but it was primarily the company's focus was all driving enterprise deals, getting to that next level of maturity. Then in 2019, I think we started to see that when we looked beneath the surface, the fundamentals of the self-service business weren't looking as healthy as they used to be.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们看到，虽然团队还在做，但公司整体的注意力都放在了拿下企业大单、把成熟度推向新高度上。然后到了 2019 年，我们开始往深处看，发现自助服务业务的健康度已经不如从前了。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think the biggest thing as we dug into it was a little bit to what we were talking about earlier with the motivation and complaints terms is it was getting harder to understand what the next generation of Slack customers really wanted from the product. Whether you're thinking about this as crossing the chasm or moving from kind of early adopters to the needs, the more majority or later adopters, I think we're at that point where not every technologically sophisticated company on earth was using Slack, but most were, and we were getting into a market that customers just had different needs. They had different levels of sophistication.
turns.zh: 我们深挖下去，最大的发现有一点呼应了前面聊到的动机和抱怨——就是越来越难搞清楚下一代 Slack 客户到底想要什么。不管是把它理解为跨越鸿沟，还是从早期采用者转向更主流、更晚采用的那批用户的需求，我觉得我们当时就处在那个节点：地球上不是每一家技术成熟的公司都在用 Slack 了，但大多数已经在了，于是我们开始进入一批需求不同的客户市场，他们的成熟度也不同。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: We did a lot of user research. We looked at all these cohort curves, which you can imagine suddenly they're like, "Huh, they're not as healthy as they used to be like. What's going on?" I think we got a bunch of insights from it. But I think really what we want to change about how we were operating was instead of to continue to try to optimize the things that had worked over the last couple years, we said, "Okay. Let's throw the whole roadmap away and instead let's come up with a bunch of hypotheses about what could be new levers that could actually help based on the insights that we now have about the next set of customers."
turns.zh: 我们做了大量用户研究，看了各种同期群曲线，你完全可以想象那种感觉：嘿，怎么不像以前那么健康了，怎么回事？我们从中得到了不少洞察。但真正改变我们运作方式的，是我们不再继续优化过去几年奏效的那些东西，而是说：好，我们把整个路线图推倒重来，根据现在对下一批客户的新认知，提出一堆假设，看看哪些是新杠杆，真的能起作用。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: "We're going to try to quickly learn which of these levers are real and which of these are just totally off the mark." We had to say for the next six months, we're probably not going to drive any impact at all. It's only going to be about learning. But at the end of that, hopefully we wind up finding a couple different levers that had years of room run and that's what wound up happening.
turns.zh: 我们要快速试出这些杠杆里哪些是真的、哪些是彻底跑偏的。我们得说清楚：接下来半年，我们可能根本不会产生任何业务影响，只为学习。但半年之后，希望我们能找到几个还有好几年增长空间的杠杆——事实证明确实如此。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: We wound up doubling the rate of our new pay customer growth in the year and a couple years after that and accelerating the self-service business. I think it really came from stepping back, being humble, not feeling like we deserve to have every company on earth sign up and then figuring out how to optimize for learning. In the long term you could get the impact.
turns.zh: 那一年以及之后几年，我们把新增付费客户的增速提高了一倍，并重新加速了自助服务业务。我觉得关键就在于退一步、保持谦逊，不要觉得地球上有每家公司都理所应当该来注册我们，然后去优化学习。长期来看，影响自然就来了。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But knowing that for the next couple quarters we're going to sacrifice impact for the sake of learning. I think that was a good muscle to build, but it was definitely not easy to do at the time.
turns.zh: 不过也要知道，接下来的几个季度我们要为学习而牺牲业务影响。我觉得这确实是值得锻炼的一种能力，但当时做起来绝对不容易。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, the story begs the question, what are the levers that worked? Whatever you can share.
turns.zh: 嗯，这个故事让人忍不住想问：到底哪些杠杆奏效了？能分享的尽量分享一下。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: One of the big things that we wound up focusing on is what we talk about is comprehension, desirability. The fundamental challenge I think for new users or new teams using your product once you get past the kind of tech early adopters is do they comprehend what this thing is for? Do they understand how it works? Then desirability is why should they care? Most people at work are not like," Hey. You know what I want to do today is start using an entirely new tool and convince all my coworkers to get on board.
turns.zh: 我们最终聚焦的一个大头，就是我们前面聊到的：理解度，以及渴望度。我认为，一旦过了技术早期采用者这一阶段，新用户或新团队使用你产品时最根本的挑战就是：他们理解这东西是干嘛的吗？他们懂它怎么用吗？而渴望度则是：他们为什么要关心它？大多数人上班的时候可不会想，嘿，我今天最想干的事就是开始用一整套全新工具，还得说服所有同事都上车。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: That is not part of your job. Your job has goals and measurements and everything else. Really ... understanding that. How do you push on that in that new user experience? It sounds maybe a little ludicrous, but Slack always has a free product. Obviously, there's a free tier that you can use, but we had never actually figured out a trial strategy where we actually gave you a taste of the paid product.
turns.zh: 那本不在你的工作范围内。你的工作有目标、有考核，还有别的一堆事。真正理解这一点之后，你怎么在新用户体验里推动这件事？听起来可能有点离谱，但 Slack 一直都有免费产品。当然有免费档可以用，可我们以前从来没真正搞出一个试用策略，让你真正尝到付费产品的味道。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Either we're on the free tier or we get to pay for the paid tier. And that wound up being one of, I think the Ripest veins is figuring out how to give people a taste of the full premium Slack experience so that they would never want to go back and doing that in a variety of different points in the customer journey. Then I'd say the other biggest thing I would call the one out is we really need to figure out a new north star metric for motivating the teams across Slack.
turns.zh: 要么在免费档，要么直接付费买完整档。而那最终成了最成熟的一个方向之一：琢磨怎么让人们先尝一口完整的高级 Slack 体验，让他们再也不想回去，而且要在客户旅程的好几个不同节点上都这么做。另外一个我要单独点名的大头是，我们确实需要为整个 Slack 找到一个新的北极星指标来激励各个团队。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: At that point in time, we basically had paid customers and then we had creative teams, which is the very, very beginning, very, very end of the journey. We did a lot of quantitative research and data science and wound up coming up with this new metric we call successful teams, which is a little bit ... I feel a lot of companies have this Facebook, I'm lucky number seven or whatever it was.
turns.zh: 那时候，我们基本只有付费客户，以及创意团队——也就是旅程最最开头、最最末尾的那一小撮。我们做了大量定量研究和数据科学工作，最终搞出了一个叫成功团队的新指标，有点像……我感觉很多公司都有那种 Facebook 的七项魔法数字之类的东西。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Where what we found was that if you could get five people using Slack, the majority of the work week to just communicate at all, that would be a successful team there were going to be 400% more likely to upgrade over the next six months. That seems like a very low bar, five people to use Slack throughout the work week, not even every day. But it turns out that if you could get that level of critical mass the rest would take care of itself.
turns.zh: 我们发现的规律是：如果能有五个人在工作周里哪怕只是用 Slack 沟通，那就是一个成功团队，而这样的团队在接下来六个月里升级付费的可能性要高出 400%。这门槛听起来很低——五个人整个工作周用 Slack，甚至都不用每天都用。但事实证明，只要能达到这个临界规模，后面的事就顺理成章了。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: We wound up motivating not just the team that was focused on self-service but all these other feature teams across the company to drive more new successful teams, knowing that if we can move that which is much earlier in the funnel but not a top of funnel metric, then it would actually drive upgrades and paid customers and thus revenue long-term. That was a huge turning point for how we rally product teams around somebody to actually drive that self-service business.
turns.zh: 于是我们不只是激励专注自助服务的团队，而是让公司里所有其他功能团队都去推动更多新的成功团队——我们知道，如果能推动这个指标（它更靠漏斗上游，但也不是最顶端的指标），长期就会真正带动升级、带来付费客户，进而带来收入。这对我们如何把产品团队凝聚到自助服务业务上，是一个巨大的转折点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, this feels like its own podcast. Just to analyze the things you learned down this journey, and there's so many takeaways here. One is just the importance of an activation metric that is predictive of retention sales. It sounds like you landed on five people in a company like DAU basically for a week, something like that. That's awesome.
turns.zh: 天哪，这感觉都能单独开一档播客了。光是剖析你这一路学到的东西就够，而且收获太多了。其中一点就是：一个能预测留存和销售的激活指标太重要了。听起来你最终落到的是大约五个人、在公司里基本像 DAU 那样、持续一周之类。这点太赞了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then the other interesting takeaway here is I'm actually doing a bunch of interviews with founders of the most successful B2B companies and interestingly, not all, maybe half are like, "I still don't think we have product market fit. They're at a billion dollars valuation growing crazy." They're like, I feel like I have product market fit with the current users but I don't with the people I want next.
turns.zh: 另一个有趣的收获是，我最近正采访一批最成功 B2B 公司的创始人，有意思的是，并不是所有人都这样，大概一半人会说：我到现在还是觉得我们没真正找到产品市场契合。他们估值都已经十亿美金、增长疯狂了，却说：我觉得对现在的用户是契合了，但对我想拿下的下一批人还没契合。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: That's exactly right. I think that's exactly right. I think of product market fit is almost like you keep stacking these S-curves where you get product market fit in a small group and then you suddenly reach exponential growth because you can crack that coal group, that type of audience, but then you start declining because you start hitting the ceiling of, we've got in, I don't know what it might be every development team in the US to be using this product.
turns.zh: 完全正确。我觉得就是这么回事。我觉得产品市场契合有点像你不断堆叠一条条 S 曲线：你在一个小群体里找到契合，然后因为撬动了那类人群而迎来指数级增长；但随后你开始下滑，因为你撞到了天花板——比如美国所有的开发团队都用上我们的产品了，差不多到头了。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Then you jump up to the next S-curve, which is like how do we get technology savvy teams that aren't developers or how do we get people who are in large eventerprises who are outside the US. Each become new curves that you have to build product market fit for. I think it's just all a huge exercise in being self-critical, being humble, not presuming that you've cracked this thing forever and keeping kind of a very beginner's mindset of what does the next audience need. "
turns.zh: 然后你跳到下一条 S 曲线，比如：怎么拿下那些不是开发者的技术敏感型团队？或者怎么拿下美国以外大型企业里的人？每一条都是一个你需要重新建立产品市场契合的新曲线。我觉得这整个就是一场保持自我批判、保持谦逊的修炼，不要假定自己已经一劳永逸地破解了这事，始终用初学者的心态去想：下一批受众需要什么？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Your previous audience. Didn't need it all.
turns.zh: 你之前那批受众，根本不需要这些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you think about the pie chart of what you had to change to make it work, how much of it was it messaging, positioning, onboarding, optimization versus product features?
turns.zh: 如果用一个饼图来看，为了让它奏效，你不得不改变的那些东西里，有多少是信息传达、定位、引导、优化，又有多少是产品功能本身？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I would say maybe 60-40 in the sense of the early journey. I mean not just obviously positioning messaging, but the entire experience of unboxing Slack if you will with your team. We called it the day one journey, but extended to really kind of day 30 in reality and it's a single player and multiplayer experience. It is really complex.
turns.zh: 我会说大概是六四开，指的是早期旅程。我指的不仅是定位和话术，而是你和团队一起开箱体验 Slack 的整个感受。我们叫它第一天旅程，但其实延伸到差不多第三十天，而且是单人加多人混合的体验，非常复杂。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But then I think what we realized was you can make that incredible, but if fundamental parts of the product were missing that would make it comprehensible to the next audience, then you're going to have problems. It sounds maybe impossible to remember, but Slack used to not have wizzywig message composition.
turns.zh: 不过后来我们意识到，就算你把那段体验做得再惊艳，如果产品里缺少一些基础功能，导致下一代受众根本理解不了它，那还是会有问题。听起来可能很难想象，但 Slack 以前连可视化消息编辑框都没有。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: You used to have to use mar, down. Making that wizzywig was a huge boost making mobile work offline so it worked no matter where you were in the world was another big one. All the things about configuring your sidebar notification so that as you scale it you should just Slack it and become overwhelming. Those are some of the foundational product investments that we wound up making so that next generation of Slack customers could get value and not be overwhelmed or daunted by it.
turns.zh: 你以前得用 Markdown。把它改成可视化编辑，是巨大的提升；让移动端能离线工作、不管你在世界哪个角落都能用，是另一大块。还有所有关于配置侧边栏通知的事，让你规模变大时不会被 Slack 淹没。这些都是我们最终做下的基础产品投入，好让下一代 Slack 客户能真正获得价值，又不会被它压垮或吓退。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe one last question along these lines, people look at Slack as maybe the first major product-led growth success story and they always look at Slack of like, "Oh, we just want to grow Slack. Let's see what they did." For people that are studying Slack's journey and success, what do you think Slack did right early on that maybe people don't recognize or don't appreciate enough that founders today should be thinking about more so versus just like let's just make a freemium product.
turns.zh: 顺着这个方向最后一个问题吧。很多人把 Slack 看作也许是第一个产品驱动增长的成功案例，总是盯着 Slack 说：哦，我们就是想照着 Slack 增长。对于那些研究 Slack 历程和成功的人来说，你觉得 Slack 早期哪些做对的事，是大家没意识到或不够重视、而今天的创始人更该去思考的——而不是简单地照抄做一个免费增值产品？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Right. I mean, I think, maybe the most telling thing is when Slack started, certainly when I joined still, I don't think a word or acronym product-led growth existed. It wasn't like we were really good at taking this playbook and applying it. I think it was more that whole term of art became a thing as maybe many other freemium SaaS products took off.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得最有说服力的也许是：Slack 刚起步时，甚至到我加入时，产品驱动增长这个词、这个缩写都还不存在。我们并不是特别擅长套用某个现成打法。我觉得更多是随着很多别的免费增值 SaaS 产品起飞，这个行业术语才慢慢成了一个概念。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Not to be repetitive. But I think the core of it really was building a product that customers loved enough that they would put their own social capital on the line to get their coworkers on board 5 to 50 people." At the time the biggest company I imagined using Slack was 50 people because I don't know how this is going to work beyond that, maybe it'll become pandemonium. Obviously, that was the initial, I think real, real strong product market fit.
turns.zh: 不想重复。但核心真的就是：打造一个客户足够热爱的产品，以至于他们愿意拿出自己的社交资本，去把同事都拉上车——5 到 50 人。当时我能想象使用 Slack 的最大公司也就 50 人，因为我不知道超过这个规模会怎样，也许就乱成一团了。显然，那是最初、也是真正强悍的产品市场契合。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But the other bit which then was what powered the enterprise business was teams of 5 to 50 people who worked at larger companies. I think what wound up happening was that you would have teams that was independently at a company like IBM or Disney or Capital One or whoever it might be, or Comcast discovering Slack using it for themselves because they thought it would just make their working lives simpler, more pleasant, more productive, and maybe not even know that anyone else at the company was using Slack.
turns.zh: 但另一块后来驱动了企业业务的，是那些在更大公司里、由 5 到 50 人组成的小团队。后来发生的是：像 IBM、迪士尼、Capital One，或者康卡斯特这类公司里，会有团队自己发现并私下用起 Slack，因为他们觉得这能让工作生活更简单、更愉快、更高效，甚至可能压根不知道公司里还有别的人在用 Slack。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Then by the time we then scaled our enterprise sales team, I mean, truly the exercise initially was just take customer domain, sort by number of active users and call them in the order of that which is, "Hey, by the way, you have a couple thousand people actually using Slack at your company. Do you want to think about a broader deployment or controls or analytics?"
turns.zh: 等我们后来扩张企业销售团队时，最初的打法简直就是：拿客户域名，按活跃用户数排序，然后按那个顺序挨个打电话——嘿，顺便说一句，你们公司其实已经有几千人在用 Slack 了，要不要考虑更大范围的部署，或者要些管控、分析功能？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think that was it. That's consumer great experience that customers love enough to get their coworkers on and pay for themselves. Then at enterprise companies like having a bunch of different flowers sprouting so that eventually you could roll up an enterprise-wide deal and then was all the tactics. But I think that that was where it started.
turns.zh: 我觉得就是这么回事：先有消费者级的绝佳体验，客户爱到愿意拉同事上车、还自己掏钱；然后在大企业里像长出一朵朵花，最后才能汇总成一笔全企业级的大单，之后才是各种战术。但起点就是那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The way you described it at the beginning of make a product that people want to share with their colleagues reminds me of a ... I was just listening to an interview with Seth Godin who's this marketing legend. I think he has a new book. He is on every podcast. He had this really great quote that the products that win are ones that you want to tell your friends about.
turns.zh: 你开头描述的那种——做个人们想跟同事分享的产品——让我想起一件事。我刚听了一期营销传奇人物 Seth Godin 的采访，他好像出了本新书，现在每个播客都能看到他。他有句特别棒的话：赢的产品，是那些你忍不住想告诉朋友的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a really simple concept. Basically, it's like it's word of mouth is how you have to win. But I think that's so true and every successful company I talk to ends up being like, "We just want to build something people want to share with their friends," even if it's growing in some other way, SEO paid feels like that's always at the root of it is you just want to tell your friends about it because you love it. Slack I think is a great example of that.
turns.zh: 概念很简单：口碑才是你必须取胜的方式。但我觉得这话太对了，我聊过的每一家成功公司最后都会说：我们就是想做出人们愿意分享给朋友的东西。哪怕它靠别的路径在增长，SEO、付费投放，根子上好像永远都是这个——你就是太爱它了，忍不住想告诉朋友。Slack 我觉得就是个绝佳例子。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think that's true. I mean obviously, there are categories of enterprise software that isn't true for in security or ...
turns.zh: 我觉得确实如此。当然，有些企业软件品类不属于这种情况，比如安全类，或者……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But even that I think if it's an awesome security product you're like, "Hey, you got to check out this century or whatever or sneak."
turns.zh: 但就算那一类，我觉得如果是个超棒的安全产品，你也会说：嘿，你一定得看看这个某家的安全方案或者别的产品。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. Good friends with Vanta's CEO Christina. I feel like they run those stories where whoever would've thought that a compliance company would be something that people raved about to their other startup friends, like, "Oh, my God. You don't want to deal with SOC's compliance? You got in Vanta. It's amazing."
turns.zh: 对。我跟 Vanta 的 CEO Christina 是好朋友。我觉得他们讲的就是这类故事——谁能想到一家合规公司会成为人们向创业圈朋友狂热安利的对象，比如：天哪，你不想自己折腾 SOC 合规？上 Vanta 啊，太神了。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. Maybe that is true. I think especially in this day and age where all the marketing acquisition channels have been so saturated, people optimizing so much, I think it's really hard to scale a big enough business if you don't have some amount of word of mouth and customer love driven growth. I think it's hard to scale it on like, "We're going to just play the cat game and in hopes that the numbers work out."
turns.zh: 对。也许真是这样。我觉得尤其在这个年代，所有营销获客渠道都极度饱和、人人都在拼命优化，如果你没有一点口碑和顾客热爱驱动的增长，很难把生意规模做起来。光靠玩数字游戏、指望账算得过来就想做大，我觉得很难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember Slack rolling out at Airbnb and all the designers getting so excited about it, creating their channels and everyone's just like, "What the hell are they doing as this thing?" Then it did exactly what you're describing just spread. Everyone's just like, "Whoa, this is cool." They're all telling each other that how useful it is to them and spread like crazy.
turns.zh: 我记得 Slack 在 Airbnb 铺开时，所有设计师都兴奋得不行，建自己的频道，大家一开始都像：这帮人在搞什么鬼？然后它恰恰就像你说的那样扩散开，所有人都哇这东西好酷，互相安利它对自己多有用，疯了一样传开。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else on Slack that you think would be interesting to share in terms of what makes it a successful product team, product business before I move on to another topic?
turns.zh: 在换话题之前，关于 Slack 还有什么有意思的、能分享它为何是个成功产品团队、成功产品生意的东西吗？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: The other thing I think is maybe a little bit interesting in terms of how we develop product and it's really different and it's changed over time, which is that obviously the easiest person to build for is yourself and the next easiest is people who look almost exactly like you or have similar preferences and sophistication. I think in the early days of Slack, that's basically what we did.
turns.zh: 另一件我觉得有点意思的，是关于我们怎么开发产品，这真的跟别家很不一样，而且随着时间也变了——最容易为其做产品的人是你自己，其次最容易的是跟你几乎一模一样、偏好和成熟度相近的人。我觉得 Slack 早期基本就是这么干的。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I mean it was really just trying to build for small technologically savvy teams in terms of you could build a pretty big business making a great product for them. Over the years, obviously, that's changed. One of the things I think that we've done, which has worked really well, one obviously is we've figured out how to do experimentation in a SaaS product, which is not always obvious because the metrics are much longer term than you land at a checkout page and then you hit Checkout.
turns.zh: 当时真的就是想为小型的技术敏感团队做产品，而光是为他们做出一款好产品，就能撑起相当可观的生意。这些年，这显然变了。我们做对的一件事，其中一个是搞清了怎么在 SaaS 产品里做实验，这并不总是一目了然，因为指标比到了结账页点一下结账要长得多。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But I think the other thing is we figured out how to scale up getting real customers using Slack in the wilds for new functionality. We have this really robust program that we call our pilot program where we have, I don't know, probably thousands of different customers that have all signed different agreements now where we can actually roll out to progressively larger user bases, because Slack is a multiplayer product.
turns.zh: 但另一件事，是我们搞清了怎么规模化地让真实客户在实战中用上 Slack 的新功能。我们有一个非常扎实的项目，叫试点计划（pilot program），大概有几千家不同的客户签了各种协议，我们可以把功能逐步推给越来越大的用户群——因为 Slack 是个多人产品。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: You often have to roll out real net new functionality to a whole company or whole team because otherwise you can't use huddles by yourself, for example. Then we have a really great program for actually getting feedback from those customers both through Slack connect itself through surveys and this winds up being a lifeblood of feature teams where you can, by the time you actually launch a big net new feature for Slack, have done so much customer feedback from people actually using in the wild to get work done and so much more confidence in what you're building from the metrics and the surveys that we do that you know can't guarantee it's going to be a hit.
turns.zh: 你经常得把全新的功能整个推给一整家公司或一个团队，否则你自己一个人是用不了 huddles（语音聊天室）的。然后我们有一个特别好的机制，能通过 Slack Connect 本身和调查问卷，从这些客户那里拿到反馈。这对功能团队来说就是生命线——等你真正发布一个 Slack 的重大新功能时，已经收集了大量真实客户在实战中拿它干活儿的反馈，加上我们做的指标和问卷带来的信心，虽然还是不能保证一定爆红。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But you can be really confident not because it just worked well internally, which is no longer that predictive, but because it worked well for a thousand different companies, in 50 different countries, in 20 different industries. I think not early on SaaS companies don't need to figure that out, but I think as you grow and as you have a more diverse customer base as you said all these SaaS founders who said, "Hey, you got to keep reestablishing product market fit."
turns.zh: 但你能很有底气，不是因为它在我们内部跑得好——那个已经不那么有预测性了——而是因为它在上千家不同公司、50 个不同国家、20 个不同行业里都跑得好。我觉得早期 SaaS 公司还不需要搞清楚这个，但随着你增长、客户群越来越多元，就像你说的那些 B2B 创始人讲的：你得不断重新建立产品市场契合。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think that is a programmatic way of being able to do that with your product development process. That's pretty interesting.
turns.zh: 我觉得这正是用产品开发流程、以系统化方式去做这件事的办法。挺有意思的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any tips for how to choose who to include in this group if someone wants to build something like this for themselves?
turns.zh: 如果有人想给自己建一套这样的东西，在挑选纳入这个群体的人方面，有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think the two most important things are you want a lot of diversity in terms of industry, company size, location and so on. I think you want to pick people who are actually motivated to want to be part of the development process and have a slightly higher risk tolerance. Not every company wants to actually be beta testing new functionality that might get removed.
turns.zh: 我觉得最重要的两点是：首先行业、公司规模、地区等方面要高度多元；其次要挑那些真的有动力、愿意参与开发过程、风险容忍度稍高的人。不是每家公司都愿意去测一个可能随时被砍掉的新功能。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Making sure we have this champion network that we built that people who love Slack enough that they're willing to put up with a little bit of pain in that rougher period are willing to have something that they try to use and then we decide actually we're going to kill that feature before we ever ship it to everybody. Diversity and pain tolerance.
turns.zh: 我们要确保建起一张拥护者网络：那些足够热爱 Slack、愿意在那段比较粗糙的时期忍受一点痛苦，愿意试用一个东西、然后我们决定在全面发布前把它砍掉的人。一句话：多元 + 能忍痛。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of something else, the CTO Stripe shared of how they build new product, which is they pick a couple customers that need a problem solved and they just build it for them essentially and with them and in B2B. Generally, it's a lot easier to build something people really want because they are very motivated for you to solve their problem and they're going to put in the time. You don't need a thousands of people involved, you just need a couple.
turns.zh: 这让我想起另一件事：Stripe 的 CTO 分享过他们怎么做新产品——挑几个有某个问题待解决的用户，基本就是为他们、和他们一起把东西做出来。在 B2B 里，通常你只要满足几个真正有动力让你解决他们问题的人，就容易做出大家真正想要的东西，因为他们会投入时间。你不需要上千人参与，几个就够了。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. I definitely think it was one of those things where if you can do it away and they say I can't live without it, the classic not ... Do you like it? Sure. But can you work without this thing? If the answer is definitely not, you've built something that probably a lot of other companies will want to.
turns.zh: 对。我绝对认为这就是那种情况：如果你能远远地做出来，而他们说我没这东西活不下去——经典的不是问喜不喜欢，而是问能不能没有它。如果答案绝对是不能，那你做出的东西大概别家公司也会想要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. I'm going to shift to a totally different topic, which could also be its own whole podcast, but let's just see how it goes. You're with this, I'd say famous blog post on product management called The 10 Traits of Great Product Managers. I want to just try to go through this list briefly and just see how it goes. This could be an hour of conversation. But let's just run through it, because I think it'd be useful for people to hear and I think these are all 100% true even though you wrote this number of years ago at this point and let's just see what comes up. Then I have a few follow-up questions on this list.
turns.zh: 好。我要切到一个完全不同的话题了，这个话题本身也能开一整档播客，不过就先看看能聊成什么样。你有一篇很有名的关于产品管理的博客文章，叫《优秀产品经理的 10 个特质》。我想就顺着这个清单快速过一遍，看看能聊出什么。这本来能聊一小时。但我们快速走一遍吧，因为我觉得对大家有用，而且这些即使你写了好些年，现在看也 100% 成立。我们就看看会冒出什么，之后我对这个清单还有几个追问。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: These traits are ... I wrote this other thing, which is the five minutes about product management, which are all the things that people think product management is and why they switch to the job and they're disappointed by. Then I was like, "Let me actually write a positive version of this," which is the things that the job actually is about. It's not a career ladder. It's not the, "Here's the structured interview things that you should interview for."
turns.zh: 这些特质是……我之前写过另一篇叫《关于产品管理的五分钟》，里面列举了人们以为产品管理是什么、以及为什么转岗进来会失望的那些事。然后我就想：干脆写个正面版本吧，也就是这工作真正是关于什么的。它不是职业阶梯，也不是那种该按结构化面试去考察的东西。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But I think it's the actual job of product management, what is it about, what does success look like? I don't think they're really in a particular order in hindsight, but I'll read them in order. Living the future and work backwards I think is very much the idea of as a PM is one thing they're responsible for. It's having a longer-term vision and time horizon. How do you carve out time to not just be what are we doing over the next two weeks.
turns.zh: 而是产品管理真正的工作——它是关于什么、成功长什么样？我觉得回想起来它们没有特定顺序，但我就按原顺序念吧。活在未来、倒推回来，我觉得这非常契合 PM 的一项责任：拥有更长期的愿景和时间跨度。你怎么挤出时间，不只是想接下来两周要干嘛，而是……

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But six months, a year, two years from now, how do you immerse yourself in them and bring ideas back, bring inspiration back to the team.
turns.zh: ……而是半年、一年、两年之后，你怎么沉浸其中，把想法和灵感带回到团队里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to just going to throw comments at as you're going through them, just add to them. I love that this is exactly Amazon's approach of work backwards, working backwards process. At Airbnb, this is actually the main thing Brian want pushed everyone to do is just think about the idealized product of a magical world where this is totally solid and then work backwards from that. Then Paul Graham talks about this, too, just live in the future and build it.
turns.zh: 我边听你念边往里加几句感想吧。我很喜欢，这简直就是亚马逊的逆向工作法（working backwards）。在 Airbnb，Brian 推着所有人做的核心事情也就是这个：先去想那个理想化的、魔法般完美的产品，然后从那倒推回来。Paul Graham 也聊过这个，就是活在未来、把它造出来。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I definitely riffed off at least the Paul Graham thing because I remember reading that essay of he thinks everyone thinks that you can get ideas by, I don't know, sitting with their co-founder laying in Dolores Park looking up at the sky and conjuring up the next unicorn or something. Definitely not how that works. You have to actually immerse yourself in the problem space and try to imagine what the future world looks like and then what's missing for people to get to that future state. Yeah. I agree.
turns.zh: 我肯定至少借用了 Paul Graham 那个说法，因为我记得读过他那篇随笔，他说大家都以为点子是靠什么办法想出来的——比如和联合创始人在 Dolores Park 躺着看天，就凭空召唤出下一个独角兽。绝对不是那么回事。你得真的沉浸到问题空间里，去想象未来世界长什么样，然后想：人们要到达那个未来状态，还缺什么？对，我同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I also saw a great tweet by [inaudible 01:04:21] the other day about how if you're working at a company with good leaders, they're never going to be sad that your vision is too big and too ambitious. If there's some reality to it that often they want that just like, "Let's go. Let's think bigger. How do we change the way we think about the future of all this stuff?"
turns.zh: 前几天我还看到 [inaudible 01:04:21] 发的一条很棒的推文，说如果你在一家有好领导的公司，他们绝不会因为你的愿景太大、太野心勃勃而沮丧。只要它有点现实根基，他们往往正想要那个：来吧，想得再大点，我们怎么重新思考这一切的未来？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. I mean that was when I was at Google, the thing I took away most from any review with Larry and Sergei was they would ask how could we get 100X the scale or how could this work for this, would seem like an outlandish use case but would push the team to think much further into the future. Yeah. I think definitely what the founders always want.
turns.zh: 对。我在 Google 时，从 Larry 和 Sergey 任何一次评审里学到最多的就是：他们会问，我们怎么才能把规模做到 100 倍？或者这东西怎么能用于那个听起来离谱的用例？这会逼着团队把目光放得更远。对，这绝对是创始人永远想要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's what Brian Chesky always said too, just like, "How do we 10X this? What would it take to 10X this idea?
turns.zh: Brian Chesky 也总这么说：我们怎么把它做到 10 倍？要 10 倍这个想法，得付出什么？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Okay. The second one, which is maybe obvious, but thinking about how do you actually amplify your team? How do you facilitate ideas? How do you create energy? How do you create momentum? A PM role I think can be a little bit unsatisfying if you're useful, where you create things yourself opposed to you are the one who's amplifying what the work that's being created by everyone else is. You have to get into that more of a facilitator mindset.
turns.zh: 好。第二条，可能显而易见，但就是：你怎么真正放大团队的能量？怎么促成好点子？怎么制造能量、制造势头？我觉得 PM 这个角色如果只想着自己造东西、而不是去放大别人创造的东西，会有一点不满足。你得进入一种更像 facilitator（助推者）的心态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I think about here is a lot of teams don't want PMs on their team or don't like PMs or don't think PMs are valuable. What I find is that just means your PMs not good because if you have a good PM, they're just going to help you do the best work of your life. They're going to help you clarify things, prioritize well, unblock you, all that stuff.
turns.zh: 我在这里想到的是：很多团队不想要 PM、不喜欢 PM、觉得 PM 没价值。但我的发现是，那只能说明你们的 PM 不行——因为一个好的 PM，只会帮你做出这辈子最棒的工作。他会帮你厘清思路、排好优先级、帮你扫清障碍，诸如此类。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Totally. I wish should find out who wrote that expression early on of PM should be mini-CEOs. I think that's the most dangerous piece of advice ever in the history of product management because I think that is how you end up having PMs who try to act like dictators instead of leaders and facilitators. Because if you're acting like that, yeah, your team can completely reject you and say I never want another PM again.
turns.zh: 完全对。我真希望能查出来最早是谁说出 PM 应该是迷你 CEO 这句话的。我觉得那是产品管理史上最危险的一条建议，因为它会让 PM 变成想当独裁者、而不是领导者和助推者。如果你那么做，团队完全可以彻底拒绝你，说我再也不要 PM 了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So many UPMs are just like, "I'm finally going to have the power, finally." If they move from engineering or some other role and then they get there like, "Oh, what the hell? Is that to convince everyone of all these things I want to do?"
turns.zh: 对。太多 PM 一上来就像：我终于有权力了，终于。尤其是从工程或其他岗位转过来，到了位置上才发现：搞什么，合着得去说服所有人接受我想做的这些事？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: That actually, I'm going to skip in a slightly different direction of the order of this post. But the fifth one that I wrote in there was your job as to facilitate the pace and quality of decision making. That is very different than you are the person who makes all the decisions. In fact, I think one of the things that PM struggled with early on is how do you actually get the team to be able to make high quality decisions quickly without you arbitrarily playing tiebreaker all the time.
turns.zh: 其实这我要稍微跳出原文的先后顺序。我写的第五条是：你的工作是促成决策的速度和质量。这跟你来拍板做所有决策，完全是两码事。事实上，我觉得 PM 早期最难熬的一点就是：你怎么让团队不用你总当和事佬、不用你每次都随便裁决，就能快速做出高质量决策。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: It's a soft art to be able to do that. But I think that is actually how you have a really healthy team dynamic instead of PM to want to say, "Okay. Now it's my turn to get to make the decisions." It's definitely not what the job is about.
turns.zh: 这要拿捏得恰到好处，是个软功夫。但我觉得那才是一个真正健康的团队动态该有的样子，而不是 PM 想着：好，现在轮到我来做决定了。那绝对不是这份工作该有的样子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What that makes me think about is I taught a course on product management at one point that I paused for now of just the core job of a PM is to figure out what's next for every single person on the team. There's this meme or GIF of a dog on a train and he's just laying the tracks as the team is moving forward ahead of them just one step at a time. To do that, this is such an important part of that is just help people make decisions, unblock them.
turns.zh: 这让我想到，我有阵子开了门产品管理课、现在先停了——课程核心就是：PM 的根本工作，是弄清楚团队里每一个人下一步该干嘛。有个梗图或 GIF 是火车上一只狗，在团队向前冲的时候，它就在一节节地铺铁轨，永远只领先一步。要做到这点，其中极重要的一部分就是帮大家做决策、帮他们扫清障碍。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Totally. I'll combine two of these together. One is you do have to have impeccable execution. This is more of a baseline thing. But I've never seen a PM who was disorganized or didn't do follow-up or wasn't clear about expectations or timelines. It's not high in Maslow's hierarchy of PM enjoyment. But I do think it's a baseline expectation.
turns.zh: 完全对。我把其中两条合起来说。一条是你确实得有无可挑剔的执行力。这更像一个底线要求。但我从没见过哪个 PM 是混乱的、不跟进的、对期望和时间线含糊不清的。它在马斯洛需求层次里不算 PM 最享受的部分，但我认为那是底线预期。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: The thing I think is more enjoyable and probably the most important thing in the long-term is focusing on impact primarily to the customer experience but also to the business. I think there's that saying growth solves all problems. I think impact solves all PM issues, which is if a team is consistently building things people love and changing the director of the business, everything else is just an input.
turns.zh: 我觉得更有意思、而且长期看最重要的，是聚焦于影响——首要是对客户体验，其次是对业务。有句话叫增长解决一切问题。我觉得影响解决一切 PM 的问题，也就是说，如果一个团队持续在造人们热爱、并且改变业务方向的东西，其他一切都只是输入项。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think that focus and understanding as your point about laying the tracks is what direction do you need to go as a team to actually drive that impact? That's probably the single thing that PM can most control.
turns.zh: 我觉得那个聚焦和你说的铺铁轨，指向的是同一个问题：作为一个团队，要驱动那个影响，你该往哪个方向走？这大概是 PM 最能掌控的单件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I always recommend exactly that if your career is not going as well as you'd hoped or you're not getting promoted, it's usually you're not delivering impact, whatever that means to the company. It may be moving a metric may mean building great product that the founders really love.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个说法。我也总是给出一模一样的建议：如果你的职业发展不如预期、或者一直升不上去，通常是你没交付影响——不管那对公司意味着什么。它可能是一个指标的移动，也可能是做出创始人真正热爱的好产品。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Main impact can mean a lot of different things. But it's so true. On the executing impeccably bucket, the way I think about that is as a great PM you need to have this aura of "I've got this." Anytime someone puts something on your plate, it's not going to fall off. You're not going to forget about it. You're not going to let a ball drop that if the more you can create this aura of "I got this," the more responsibility people are going to give you, the more impact you'll end up having, the more people want to work with you and all that.
turns.zh: 影响可以意味着很多不同的东西。但确实如此。在执行无可挑剔这一条上，我的理解是：一个出色的 PM 要散发一种我搞定了的气场。任何时候有人把事交给你，它不会掉地上，你不会忘，你不会让任何一个球漏掉。你越能营造出这种我搞定的气场，人们就越敢把更多责任交给你，你最终的影响就越大，越多人想跟你共事，等等。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. Ben Horowitz was a board member back at Foursquare. I remember he used to have this saying very Yoda of good leaders need to say what they're going to do and then do what they said. If they can't then they need to follow up and explain why. I mean that's like the amendment and I think that is what good execution looks like.
turns.zh: 对。Ben Horowitz 当年是 Foursquare 的董事会成员。我记得他常挂嘴边一句话，特别像尤达：好的领导者要说到做到；如果做不到，就得跟进并解释为什么。我觉得那就是补充条款，而那正是一个好执行该有的样子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That last point is so important. You may not be able to do all the things on your plate, but just telling people. Hey, I'm not going to get to this thing. Let's reprioritize as such a small thing you could do and really creates that, or if you got this, they're not going to forget about this thing asked you to do.
turns.zh: 最后这点太重要了。你可能没法把盘子里的每件事都做完，但只要告诉别人：嘿，这事我顾不上了，咱们重新排个优先级——就这么个小动作，就能真正建立起那种信任；或者你展现出我搞定了，他们就不会担心你忘了他们托付的事。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. You're the shock absorber for the team. You're the thing that builds people's confidence that things are going to be running smoothly and you'll get over the Navajo speed bumps and whatever else. I'll combine two or three of these that are related or just more skills. I said right well. I actually think especially as you get to more senior positions, writing is the only scalable way of having influence on a larger, larger product org.
turns.zh: 对。你是团队的减震器。你是那个让别人有信心、相信事情会平稳运转、相信你能跨过那些 Navajo 级别的坑洼的人。我再合并几条相关的、或者就是几项技能来说。我前面说到了写作，但其实我觉得尤其当你到更资深的位置，写作是对更大的产品组织施加影响力的唯一可规模化方式。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: There's a book called On Writing by Stephen King, which I recommend to literally everybody. Stephen King, you're like ... See he's not maybe the most literary critical acclaimed author, but he's a prolific author who publishes things that people love and tell their friends about and he has a great short book on the practice of writing high-quality, high-volume production.
turns.zh: 有本叫《On Writing》的书，是 Stephen King 写的，我 literally 推荐给每一个人。Stephen King 嘛，你可能觉得他不算最有文学口碑的作家，但他是个高产的作者，写的东西人们爱看、还会安利给朋友，而且他有一本很棒的薄书，讲怎么高产又高质地写作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before you move on, I'll throw a couple more books that I found useful in my writing. One is actually called On Writing Well. That's funny that they're so similarly titled, which basically every chapter is just another way to cut more from your writing. More and more parts you should cut. Interestingly, I do have a lot of guest posts in my newsletter and I find 90% of the time if I just cut the first paragraph of what they first took a crack at and jumps straight into the thing, immediately gets better. This book talks a lot about that.
turns.zh: 你往下说之前，我补几本我在写作上觉得有用的书。一本其实叫《On Writing Well》。标题这么像挺逗的，它基本上每一章都是另一种删减你文字的方式——一茬一茬地砍。有意思的是，我的 newsletter 里确实有很多客座文章，我发现十次里有九次，只要把作者初稿的第一段砍掉、直接切入正题，文章立刻变好。这本书讲了很多这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another book that is amazing for writing better is Nobody Wants to Read Your Shit by the guy that wrote The War of Art, forget his name. But that book is awesome and it's just like nobody wants to read what you're writing. Here's how to maybe make it something people want to read. Then recently I read one called Several Short Sentences or something like that. It's all about just writing short sentences and that helps a lot. There you go. Three more recommendations.
turns.zh: 另一本对写作超有帮助的是《Nobody Wants to Read Your Shit》，作者是写《The War of Art》那个人，名字我忘了。但那本书超棒，核心就是：没人在乎你想写什么，这里是如何让它变成人们想读的东西。最近我还读了一本叫《Several Short Sentences》还是什么的，通篇就是写短句，也很有帮助。喏，又多了三本推荐。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Okay. I got to read the last two. I haven't read those, but they sound perfect. Okay. Maybe I'll throw one more. Let's say we talked about this earlier, but actually read this in the post many years ago, is optimizing for the pace of learning and knowing that long-term massive thing that's going to drive impact. I think it can be hard if you're a PM for a feature team. You're part of a big company. I don't know. I'm making this up.
turns.zh: 好。最后两本我得读读，还没看过，但听起来正合我意。好。也许我再补一本。咱们前面聊过，但其实这篇文章里好些年前就写了：为学习的速度优化，知道那个长期会带来巨大影响的东西。我觉得如果你是一个功能团队的 PM、在一家大公司里，这可能会很难。我就瞎编个例子。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: You're on the AdWords team at Google and you're responsible for the bid input selector or something and probably is a whole team, honestly, now at this point. You've got such a set of blinders on that I think it can be hard to think about what else could this team become, what else could you drive beyond the thing that's right in front of you?
turns.zh: 你在 Google 的 AdWords 团队，负责那个出价输入选择器什么的，老实说到现在估计都成一整个团队了。你的视野会被蒙得那么窄，以至于很难去想：这个团队还能变成什么？除了眼前这件事，你还能驱动什么？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Optimizing for learning, being willing to take those bolder bets, knowing you can be wrong in the short-term, but that you'll learn new levers that will be really fruitful in the long-term. It's a portfolio approach to product, but I think a really important one.
turns.zh: 为学习优化、愿意下更大胆的赌注、知道短期你可能错、但长期会学到真正有果实的杠杆。这是一种产品上的组合思维，但我觉得非常关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just interviewing a product leader at Asana, Paige Costello. We were talking about how she's often the youngest person in the room and often manages people that are much older than her and more experienced than her and asked her just how do you that? How do you succeed in that environment?
turns.zh: 我刚采访了 Asana 的一位产品负责人 Paige Costello。我们聊到，她经常是房间里最年轻的人，带的人往往比她年长、比她有经验，我就问她：你是怎么做到的？怎么在这种环境里成功？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What she's found is just being the person that has the answers and the insights in meetings, people obviously run to her like, "Hey, what do you think of this?" Because she just knows what people are going to need. I think that's exactly what you're talking about here is just be the person that knows the most about the problem, the customers, the space.
turns.zh: 她的发现就是：做那个在会议里有答案、有洞察的人，人们自然会跑来找她：嘿，你觉得这个怎么样？因为她就是知道大家会需要什么。我觉得这恰恰就是你说的——做那个对问题、对客户、对这个领域知道得最多的人。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. Then I'll combine the last two just because I know time. But the combination of ... I wrote data fluency, which is not to say that every PM needs to be a statistician. I mean it's great. I mean you've had a lot of great posts about how to understand some of the basics of experimentation, correlation, causation and statistical significance. That's all great.
turns.zh: 对。最后两条我合起来说，因为我知道时间紧。组合是……我写了数据素养（data fluency）。这不是说每个 PM 都得是统计学家。当然那也很好。你写过很多好文章，讲怎么理解实验、相关性、因果、统计显著性这些基础。那些都很好。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: But by data fluency, I think it's more actually what you were just saying, which is you know enough about the insights about your customers that it can then inform making higher likelihood product bets and that data can be quantitative, that data can be survey based, it can be from doing 100 meetings with customers yourself. Those are all types of data inputs to me. Being really fluent and then maybe combining that with great product taste.
turns.zh: 但数据素养，我觉得更像是你刚说的那个：你对客户足够有洞察，以至于能据此下出概率更高的产品赌注；而那数据可以是定量的，可以是问卷式的，也可以是你自己做了 100 场客户访谈得来的。对我而言这些都是数据输入。真正吃透它，再也许把它和优秀的产品品味结合起来。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I know it's a controversial statement now to say that there is taste for product. But I do think in all the love of the frameworks and the analytics and everything else and in the field of product, I think people sometimes lose sight of, "It's a creative field." It's not art on its own. But you could get all the inspiration from art and I actually think there's a lot ... there's a book, I think it's called Creative Selection, I forget the exact name of it, about some of the early iPhone development teams at Apple and working with Steve Jobs there.
turns.zh: 我知道现在说产品品味是个有争议的说法。但我确实觉得，在所有人痴迷框架、分析、以及各种产品方法论的同时，人们有时忘了：这是一门创造性工作。它自己不是艺术，但你完全可以从艺术里汲取灵感。其实我觉得……有本书，好像叫《Creative Selection》，确切名字我忘了，讲的是苹果早期 iPhone 开发团队、和 Steve Jobs 共事的那段。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I've never worked at Apple. But I actually think it's the best book I've read about the just iterating creative work of building new products and what it means to have taste, which is to say you've developed some amount of intuition for what people will likely love before you're able to test it. Anyway, I think taste plus fluency and data, that too is a combination, is a pretty powerful combo.
turns.zh: 我没在苹果干过。但我真心觉得那是我读过的、关于构建新产品这种创造性迭代工作、以及什么叫有品味的最好的一本书——也就是说，在还没法测试之前，你已对某些人可能会爱上的东西培养出了一点直觉。总之，品味加数据素养，这俩组合也是一个相当强悍的搭配。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me ask you just a couple questions about this list before we get to a very exciting lightning round and I can let you go.
turns.zh: 在进到超精彩的快问快答、然后放你走之前，关于这个清单我想先问你几个问题。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Of these 10 attributes, say you're a new product manager, if you had to pick two or three that you think are most important to get right and focus on in your early career, which would you say they would be?
turns.zh: 这 10 个特质里，假设你是一个刚入行的产品经理，如果只能挑两三个你认为最该做对、最该在职业生涯早期聚焦的，你会选哪几个？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think for early on in your career, what I would say is getting great at execution. It's a thing that you can most control. Then I think building that news for impact, even if the impact is more local, because that's how you actually will demonstrate momentum and build credibility and then actually do think early on getting really fluent on the data and the research side that you can have insights that you can read back to your team.
turns.zh: 我觉得在职业早期，最该说的是把执行力练到极好——这是你最能掌控的事。然后是建立对影响的嗅觉，哪怕那影响更局部，因为那正是你展现势头、建立可信度的途径；再到真的在数据和研究侧变得很熟练，让你能带回团队一些洞察。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Those are to me the most slammed up ways of becoming someone who starts to build credibility as a product manager in any organization.
turns.zh: 对我来说，这些就是成为那种在任何组织里都开始建立可信度的最扎实路径。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's what I always tell on new PMs too, is just get really good at execution because that creates that aura of, "Oh, this person's just killing it. They're just shipping on time. People know it's happening. They're hitting dates," things like that.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这也是我总跟新 PM 说的：就把执行力练到极致，因为它能营造出那种气场——哦，这人简直杀疯了，按时交付、大家知道进度、踩中节点，诸如此类。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The last question is just say more of a senior product leader, say, on director. Are there three other attributes you think are ones they should focus on most or maybe the same?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，假设是一个更资深的产品负责人，比如总监级。有没有另外三个你认为他们最该聚焦的特质，还是说一样？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. I mean I think this is where the pace and quality decision making starts to matter a lot more because you're still unresponsible sometimes for teams of teams and you're helping to facilitate high quality decisions, often ones that have a lot of uncertainty or risk or ambiguity. How do you keep the organization unblocked, not just a team moving well.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得到了这个层级，决策的速度和质量就开始重要得多，因为你有时候要对多个团队负责，你要帮着促成高质量的决策，而那往往充满不确定性、风险或模糊性。你怎么让整个组织不被卡住，而不只是让一个团队跑顺。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think the living in the future and working backwards, I think the more senior you get, it's always going to be the product founder who is responsible for the ultimate vision, but you become more responsible for that meeting a longer-term strategy to realize that vision. Becoming just someone who can dedicate more of your time to be out of the fray of the day-to-day and think more about the longer-term strategy that you want to pursue.
turns.zh: 我觉得活在未来、倒推回来，你越资深，终极愿景终究是产品创始人在负责，但你会对接一个更长期的战略、去实现那个愿景这件事，负起更多责任。你要成为那个能拨出更多时间、跳出日常纷争、去想你真正想追求的长期战略的人。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: The last one, and we talked about just earlier, but I think being a really good writer, it is just the highest leverage usage of your time. If you want to influence an organization at least for one that doesn't just spend all day in meetings, but I think it's really hard to dedicate the time to it because you're probably spending most of your day in meetings. It's the antidote to that to scale your ability to influence the product direction and maybe even the principles and how you develop product at a company.
turns.zh: 最后一条，我们前面聊过，但就是：做一个真正好的写作者，这是对你时间杠杆最高的一件事。如果你想影响一个组织——至少是影响一个不全天泡在会议里的组织——我觉得很难挤出时间写，因为你一天大半都在开会。但写作正是那帖解药，能规模化你影响产品方向、甚至影响原则和产品开发方式的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好，说到这，我们到了超精彩的快问快答环节。我有六个问题，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 来吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你最经常推荐给别人的是哪两三本书？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: These may not be the most unique, but I will say them, which is Innovator's Dilemma by Clayton Christiansen, whether you're working a large company and you're suffering it or you're working a startup and you're trying to out flank an incumbent, I still do think that and innovative solution, the follow on are the best books on product strategy to read.
turns.zh: 这些可能不算最独特，但我还是要说：Clayton Christiansen 的《创新者的窘境》（The Innovator's Dilemma），不管你在大公司正受其苦，还是在创业公司想侧翼包抄在位者，我依然觉得它以及续作是关于产品战略最好读的书。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: If you're moving into more of a leadership or management position, I think Radical Candor by Kim Scott is just incredible and worth everyone reading. Frankly, if you're a PM and you're doing soft influence, I think it's really important. Then the third one, which is maybe a little off the beat of path, there's a book called Leadership in Turbulent Times by Doris Goodwin who's a presidential historian.
turns.zh: 如果你正转向更多领导或管理岗，我觉得 Kim Scott 的《 Radical Candor》（极限坦诚）简直神作，值得人人都读。说真的，如果你是个做柔性影响力的 PM，我觉得这特别重要。第三本可能有点偏门，有本叫《Leadership in Turbulent Times》（动荡时代的领导力），作者是总统历史学家 Doris Goodwin。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: It's this amazing book that looks at four of the most notable presidents and how their leadership style evolved when they were in really critical hard times in their presidency. I just think it's actually the best book about leadership style and how do you evolve and how do you deal with crises, which again is maybe later on in your career. But I love getting inspiration from not just reading books about tech and product and I think that's one of the best ones.
turns.zh: 这本书超棒，它研究了四位最知名的总统，以及他们的领导风格在总统任内最危急艰难的时刻是怎么演变的。我就觉得它其实是关于领导风格、关于你怎么进化、怎么应对危机最好的一本书——这也许更偏职业生涯后期。但我喜欢从非科技非产品的书里汲取灵感，而这一本就是最好的之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite recent movie or TV show you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 你最近特别喜欢的一部电影或剧集是什么？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: The obvious answer, which I'm sure many people would say would be Succession. I'm not going to ruin anything for the finale because people haven't seen it all. But the writing, the Shakespearean level drama of it all, it's just incredible and just heart wrenching that you wind up loathing most of the characters. But you can't take yourself out of it.
turns.zh: 最显而易见的答案，我猜很多人都会说是《继承之战》（Succession）。我不剧透大结局，因为有人还没看完。但它的剧本、那种莎士比亚级别的戏剧张力，简直不可思议，而且让人心碎——到头来你几乎厌恶里面大多数角色，却还是停不下来。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: The one that's maybe less common, and I watched right when we started paternity leave is The Bear, I don't know if you heard about it.
turns.zh: 另一部可能没那么常见、我正好在休陪产假时看的是《熊家餐馆》（The Bear），不知道你听没听过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The restaurants.
turns.zh: 那家餐厅的。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Seen that. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对，看过。嗯。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I'm a sucker for incredible cinematography, just what they do in basically the single room of this restaurant and kitchen and just the piece of it. I think it's just an incredible piece of art. I don't know if it's the best show ever, but it is a really moving, emotionally jarring piece of TV.
turns.zh: 我是那种会被绝佳摄影迷住的人，他们基本就在这间餐厅厨房的单个空间里拍，那种质感，我觉得就是一件不可思议的艺术品。我不知道它是不是史上最好剧集，但它确实是一部动人、情绪上极具冲击力的电视作品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also, quite stressful to watch.
turns.zh: 而且，看着还挺让人紧张。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Very sure. I would not relax to it to go to sleep.
turns.zh: 非常对。我绝对不会睡前拿来放松。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But Awesome. Okay. Favorite interview question that you'd like to ask candidates?
turns.zh: 好，太棒了。你最喜欢问候选人的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: That would depend a lot, I think on obviously, the seniority level and things like that. But I think the more general, and I always love to ask people is what unfair secrets have you learned to improve the velocity and energy level of a product team? When I say unfair or you in secret, I usually mean not something that you probably read on a medium input. But what did you learn? How did you learn it and how does it work and how do you apply it? You also just get amazing interesting bits of inspiration from asking that.
turns.zh: 那要看很多因素，比如资历层级之类。但一个更通用的、我总是爱问别人的是：你学到了哪些不公平的秘诀，能提升产品团队的速度和能量？我说不公平或秘诀，通常指不是你在某篇 Medium 文章上读来的那种；而是你到底学到了什么、怎么学到的、它怎么运作、你怎么应用它？问这个，你还能收获特别有意思的灵感碎片。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 你最近发现、并爱上的一个最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: This will also serve for recommendations for you based on or you've not thread about parenting clients because none of the products I've learned or loved recently have been software. But they're all maybe software enabled. The Nanit, which is a weird name, but it's this AI-enabled camera for basically watching your day as they sleep. It's like incredible, look, because you sleep analytics and really helps you be a less neurotic parent. I would highly recommend it.
turns.zh: 这个也能算给你的一个推荐，前提是你没聊过育儿类话题——因为我最近喜欢或学到的产品没有一个是软件，但它们都算是软件赋能的。一个是 Nanit，名字怪怪的，但它是一个 AI 赋能的摄像头， basically 用来盯着宝宝睡觉。它超棒，会给你睡眠分析，真的帮你变成一个不那么神经质的家长。我强烈推荐。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: The SNOO, which is basically this amazing device that can help soothe your kid when all they need is a little bit of that soothing while they sleep so that you can sleep a little bit more. You can tell the steam here is sleep. The last one is there's this chemical up baby that has this whole elaborate stroller system with interchangeable parts and, honestly, it's just an incredibly well-designed piece of hardware that works in and out of the car.
turns.zh: 还有 SNOO，基本就是个神器，能在宝宝只需要一点安抚就能睡着时帮你哄睡，好让你多睡一会儿。你看这边的线索都是睡眠。最后一个是 Uppababy 的一款，有一整套可换零件的手推车系统，说真的，就是一件设计极好的硬件，上车下车都好使。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. I think I've re-appreciated really well-designed hard products that are not necessarily hardware from Apple and that has been what baby new parents is about.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得我重新欣赏了那些设计很好的实体产品——不一定是苹果出的硬件——而这恰恰就是新手爸妈的世界。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have all three. Also, a huge shout-out to the Nanit team who sent me a Nanit and all the stuff around the Nanit. Thank you. I'm not going to name the specific PM who sent it to me, because I don't remember his name off the top of my head, but thank you, Nanit.
turns.zh: 这三样我全有。也大力鸣谢 Nanit 团队，他们送了我一台 Nanit 和周边一堆东西。谢谢你们。我就不点名具体哪位 PM 送的，因为一时想不起他名字了，但谢谢你，Nanit。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: Yeah. It turned out there was a whole world of baby tech, which I had no idea. I mean, it makes sense that existed, but you never know about until you're a parent. Now, I'm obsessed.
turns.zh: 对。结果发现有整整一个婴儿科技的世界，我以前完全不知道。我的意思是它存在很合理，但你不当父母根本不会知道。现在，我着迷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One tip that for Nanit, my wife and I have been playing with different names for our kid and we have been changing his name in the Nanit so that anytime we go into the room it sends us a push, "Hey, there's activity in the room with the names so that we could feel the different names."
turns.zh: 关于 Nanit 有个小技巧：我和我老婆一直在拿不同的名字试我们的宝宝，我们就不断在 Nanit 里改他的名字，这样每次进房间，它都会推一条消息：嘿，房间里有个叫某名的活动。好让我们感受不同名字的感觉。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I love that. Yeah. My wife and I did something similar where we had three or four final name contenders and we didn't use the Nanit for. But we literal just picked a week and said, "On Monday we're going to like refer to the future baby by that name for the entire week and give some personification to it." That helped us get down from four to one. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。对。我和我老婆也干过类似的事：我们留了三四个决赛名字，没用 Nanit，但就真挑了一周，说周一开始就整周用那个名字指代未来的宝宝，给它一点人格化。那帮我们从四个减到一个。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a wide-ranging set of pieces of advice we got on this podcast. Two more questions. What is something relatively minor you've changed in how you develop product at Slack that has had a lot of impact on your ability to execute?
turns.zh: 这期播客里我们聊了一组跨度极广的建议。还有两个问题。在 Slack 里，你改了某个相对微小、却极大提升你执行能力的事情是什么？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: By far, the biggest thing, which is more of a cultural shift is that we stopped spending so many cycles on design explorations of static mocks or walkthroughs and said, "How quickly can we get into prototyping the path in real software, even if it's messy and you throw it away," at least for something like Slack. You got to live and touch and smell the software. You can't just look at it. That's been a huge unlock for avoiding spending months on design debates and just getting to, well, how does the software feel? That's what matters.
turns.zh: 到目前为止最大的一件事，更像一次文化转向：我们不再把那么多周期花在静态稿或走查的设计探索上，而是说，我们多快能进到真实软件里把那条路径做成原型——哪怕它很乱、最后会扔掉——至少对 Slack 这类产品，你必须去摸、去用、去感受这个软件，不能只看着它。这对避免花几个月吵设计、直接进入到软件到底什么感觉，是个巨大的解锁。那才是关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of Slack, final question, what is your favorite Slack pro tip that people may not be aware of?
turns.zh: 说到 Slack，最后一个问题：你最爱的、人们可能不知道的 Slack 使用技巧是什么？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I'm going to give two because if someone asks me this, "I'm like, these are the two things that if you're not in love with Slack, you'll fall in love with Slack." The first is obviously you have a sidebar, it can be unruly, but you can customize the sidebar into sections and each of those sections you can have settings like. "Show unread only" or "Sort by recency," or "Sort by alphabetical," whatever it might be. You can collapse the section so you don't see it all at once.
turns.zh: 我给两个，因为有人这么问我时我会说：这两样，如果你还没爱上 Slack，会让你爱上它。第一个显然是你有个侧边栏，它可能很乱，但你可以把侧边栏自定义成区块，每个区块都能设像显示未读、按最近活动排序、按字母排序之类的设置。你还能折叠区块，不用一次全看见。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think having a well-managed sidebar, which doesn't actually take that long, it's like this amazing thing because then all this inbound is structured in an order and a grouping that fits how you want to view your working life. Customizing the sidebar. The second thing is just use the quick switcher for everything. Just hit Apple K and just start typing and it feels like they're playing a video game, just hopping around channels, people, files, search. Pretty much all the actions you can take are on as well.
turns.zh: 我觉得有个管理得当的侧边栏，其实花不了多少时间，却像件神器，因为所有涌入的信息都被按你想要的顺序和分组结构化了。自定义侧边栏。第二件事就是凡事用快捷切换器（quick switcher）。按一下 Cmd+K 就开始打字，感觉像在打电子游戏，在频道、人、文件、搜索之间跳来跳去。基本所有操作都在上面。

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I think most SaaS products now have borrowed that pattern. You can use another software, but it works particularly well in Slack.
turns.zh: 我觉得现在大多数 SaaS 产品都借用了这个模式。你用别的软件也能用到，但它在 Slack 里尤其好使。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No. I know the last thing you needed was to record a podcast your first week back to work. I so appreciate you making the time. It feels like we're two ships passing in the night from pat leave and to new pat leave. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and learn more and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 不。我知道你最不需要的就是回岗第一周就来录播客。我特别感激你抽时间。感觉我们就像两艘在夜里错过的船，一个刚结束陪产假、一个刚要开始。最后两个问题：大家如果想联系你、多了解你，能在网上哪里找到你？听众又能怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: Noah Weiss
turns.en: I will confess that I haven't used Twitter in months because I was doing digital detox, but still I think @Noah_Weiss is a pretty good place to find me online and whether there or anywhere else, still love to have peoples like Slack feature requests, especially about things that you wish were possible or that would get the rest of your company to join on Slack because you love it, but you can't convince them. Those are always golden nuggets.
turns.zh: 我得坦白，我好几个月没用 Twitter 了，因为我在做数字排毒，但 @Noah_Weiss 依然是个能找到我的好地方；不管在那还是别处，我还是很爱听大家提 Slack 的功能需求，尤其是那种你希望它能做到、或者能帮你说服公司其他人也用上 Slack 的事——因为你爱它，却说服不了他们。那些永远都是金子般的宝物。

turns.zh: 太棒了。Noah，非常感谢你来到这里。
